title: The Naked Gun: From the Files of Police Squad!
logline: Leslie Nielsen as deadpan Lt. Frank Drebin. Zucker-Abrahams-Zucker gag-a-second spoof of cop shows.
overview: When the bumbling Lieutenant Frank Drebin investigates events following the shooting of his partner, he stumbles upon an attempt to assassinate Queen Elizabeth II.
tagline: You've read the ad, now see the movie!

jokes.text: Opening scene: Frank Drebin bursts into a secret terrorist summit featuring Idi Amin, Muammar Gaddafi, Yasser Arafat, Ayatollah Khomeini, and other real-world villains gathered in one room, presented as a mundane meeting
jokes.setup: A serious-looking summit of the world's most feared terrorists discussing global humiliation of America with deadly earnestness
jokes.punchline: The entire gathering is treated as a mundane boardroom disagreement, with Drebin crashing it like a beat cop busting a card game
jokes.explanation: ZAZ's signature move: placing the deadpan in the most extreme possible context. The gap between the gravity of the attendees (actual world villains) and the mundane bickering tone is enormous. The concept alone earns high marks — it's bold, original, and immediately establishes the film's anarchic register.

jokes.text: "What? And spoil three years of good PR? The Americans believe I'm a nice guy. In some of their polls, I'm more popular than their president!"
jokes.setup: Other terrorists advocate wiping out Washington and New York
jokes.punchline: Gaddafi objects not on moral grounds but because he's carefully cultivated a positive American PR image and doesn't want to blow it
jokes.explanation: Genuinely sharp political satire embedded in absurdist context. The joke works on multiple levels: it satirizes media spin, political polling, and the gap between public image and private reality. The specificity ('three years of good PR') elevates it above a generic 'villain wants to look good' gag. Comparable in wit to the 8.0 anchor — highly quotable and zeitgeist-aware for 1988.

jokes.text: "Hey, who are you? / I'm Lieutenant Frank Drebin, Police Squad. And don't ever let me catch you guys in America!"
jokes.setup: Frank has just single-handedly beaten up every terrorist in the room in what was clearly an over-the-top brawl
jokes.punchline: His parting warning — 'don't ever let me catch you guys in America' — is a comically toothless threat delivered with total authority, as if he's scolding jaywalkers
jokes.explanation: The perfect encapsulation of Drebin's character: total confidence, zero self-awareness, absurdly understated response to a world-historical situation. 'Don't let me catch you guys in America' is a line a small-town sheriff might say to teenagers — applied here to global terrorists. Economy is near-perfect. This is classic Nielsen deadpan and one of the film's signature early moments.

jokes.text: "It's a great day for Americans. This man alone..." — newsreel/announcer style narration cut short as the crowd ignores Frank completely
jokes.setup: Frank returns home apparently as a hero; a narrator begins building him up with triumphant language
jokes.punchline: The crowd at the airport is entirely there for 'Weird Al' Yankovic and doesn't notice Frank at all
jokes.explanation: Classic ZAZ misdirection/deflation structure: build up the hero's triumphant return, then reveal the entire crowd is there for 'Weird Al' Yankovic. The specific choice of Weird Al as the deflating celebrity is inspired — he's just famous enough to be recognizable and just odd enough to be funny. Well-constructed.

jokes.text: "I want to know one thing - is it true about Victoria?" / "I'm afraid so. She ran off with some guy. They got married last week." / "Then it's over. All of this is meaningless. I did it for her. Everything."
jokes.setup: Frank has just returned from a heroic mission in Beirut; his colleague congratulates him
jokes.punchline: Frank's first question is about his ex — his dramatic heartbreak speech ('I did it for her. Everything.') plays as bathos against the backdrop of international heroism
jokes.explanation: Good bathos — Frank's self-pity undercuts the heroic moment nicely. The joke works because Frank is completely sincere; it's character-driven comedy about a man whose emotional priorities are hilariously skewed.

jokes.text: "Do any of you understand how a man can hurt inside?" / "Frank, they're not here for you. 'Weird Al' Yankovic is on the plane."
jokes.setup: Frank delivers an emotional speech about heartbreak to the assembled press crowd at the airport, believing they're there to see him return as a hero
jokes.punchline: He's been pouring his heart out to a crowd that is entirely there for Weird Al Yankovic and couldn't care less about him
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed misdirection. The setup lets us believe the crowd is there for Frank, amplifying his emotional speech. The reveal (Weird Al) is perfectly timed and also a funny celebrity cameo in its own right. The economy is excellent — the punchline is six words and demolishes everything that came before it. Among the stronger gags in this reel.

jokes.text: "Just that he's an Olympic gymnast and it's the best sex she's ever had."
jokes.setup: Frank asks what he knows about the man his ex-wife ran off with, expecting vague or comforting non-information
jokes.punchline: Ed provides the most brutally specific and devastating detail possible in the most matter-of-fact tone
jokes.explanation: Classic ZAZ oversharing played deadpan. The joke is entirely in the specific detail — 'Olympic gymnast' (implying extreme physical capability) + 'best sex she's ever had' delivered flatly by a friend who clearly doesn't understand why this information is cruel. Near-perfect economy. The two-beat structure (gymnast → best sex ever) adds escalation within a single sentence.

jokes.text: "He's got a 50/50 chance of living, though there's only a 10% chance of that."
jokes.setup: Doctor delivers a grave medical prognosis about Nordberg's survival chances
jokes.punchline: The doctor confidently qualifies '50/50' with 'though there's only a 10% chance of that' — a statistically nonsensical statement delivered with clinical authority
jokes.explanation: One of the great ZAZ one-liners. The structure is mathematically absurd but delivered with total medical seriousness — it sounds like it means something while meaning nothing at all. The rhythm is perfect: the first clause sets a recognizable prognosis format, the second clause destroys it with cheerful illogic. Highly quotable, endlessly reusable in conversation. This is legitimately close to the 9.5 craft anchor in terms of construction, though slightly below in cultural footprint.

jokes.text: "Mrs Nordberg, I think we can save your husband's arm. Where would you like it sent?"
jokes.setup: Frank opens with apparent medical reassurance: 'we can save your husband's arm'
jokes.punchline: The follow-up question reveals the arm has already been amputated and they're asking about shipping it — the reassurance was meaningless
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in misdirection and dark comedy. 'We can save your husband's arm' is reassuring on its own. The follow-up question ('where would you like it sent?') recontextualizes it as a severed-limb logistics inquiry. The gap between the comforting setup and the horrifying logical implication is enormous and lands perfectly dark. Near top-tier ZAZ construction.

jokes.text: Phone ringing at Nordberg's hospital bedside — Frank picks it up and begins a cheerful conversation while Nordberg is in critical condition
jokes.setup: Dramatic, tense hospital scene with Nordberg on life support; Frank rushes to help with the medical equipment
jokes.punchline: The phone rings and Frank reflexively answers it, completely breaking the emotional moment with bureaucratic normalcy
jokes.explanation: A reliable ZAZ visual/physical beat — the interruption of a serious moment by mundane normalcy. Works because of Drebin's character (he'd answer it) but is more of a functional gag than an exceptional one. The transcript doesn't give us what he says, limiting the analysis.

jokes.text: "Get the switch at the back of the bed!" — Frank apparently rips out or scrambles the medical equipment
jokes.setup: Nordberg is in critical condition; Frank is trying to help with the medical equipment
jokes.punchline: Frank's attempt to help makes things worse — classic incompetent-hero physical comedy
jokes.explanation: Functional physical comedy inferred from context. The transcript gives minimal detail; the hospital equipment slapstick is a reliable beat but not especially inventive in conception.

jokes.text: "Get the switch at the back of the bed!" — Frank frantically tries to manage Nordberg's hospital equipment, implying comedic chaos with wires/machines
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to help the dying Nordberg; medical equipment is involved
jokes.punchline: Frank's inept interference with hospital machinery — the visual chaos of a cop fumbling with life support
jokes.explanation: Inferred physical comedy — Frank messing with hospital equipment is a classic slapstick setup. Without the visual it's hard to fully score, but the concept is functional if not inspired.

jokes.text: "I love you." / "I love you, too, Nordberg. Who were they?"
jokes.setup: Nordberg is trying desperately to communicate the name of a ship; Frank leans in expecting vital police intelligence
jokes.punchline: What comes out instead is 'I love you' — which Frank accepts sincerely and returns without missing a beat before resuming the interrogation
jokes.explanation: Sweet and funny simultaneously. Frank's unselfconscious 'I love you, too' is perfectly in character — he's so earnest he just goes with it. The immediate pivot back to 'who were they?' keeps the comedic rhythm tight. Good character integration.

jokes.text: "Ship... Boat..." / "That's right. A boat. When you're better, we'll go sailing together, just like last year."
jokes.setup: Nordberg is trying to give Frank a vital clue about a ship; Frank leans in to interpret each word as a dying clue
jokes.punchline: Frank interprets 'boat' as a sentimental invitation to go sailing rather than a lead
jokes.explanation: Part of a running escalating gag where Frank consistently misinterprets Nordberg's dying clues in the most literal/sentimental way. Each beat adds to the cumulative comedic build. This is the first step in an escalating sequence — decent on its own, better in context.

jokes.text: "No... Drugs." / "Nurse, give this man some drugs! Can't you see he's in pain? Give him a shot, quickly!"
jokes.setup: Nordberg tries to say 'drugs' as the next clue; Frank interprets every word as a request rather than information
jokes.punchline: Frank orders the nurse to administer drugs, believing Nordberg is asking for pain relief, not identifying a drug smuggling operation
jokes.explanation: The escalating misinterpretation sequence continues and gets better. Frank's frantic call for the nurse ('Can't you see he's in pain?') while Nordberg is literally trying to report a drug crime is a great ironic inversion. The pace accelerates nicely.

jokes.text: "Heroin! Heroin, Frank!" / "Nordberg, that's a pretty tall order. Give me a couple of days on that one."
jokes.setup: Nordberg finally gets out 'heroin' as the key clue; Frank has been misinterpreting everything so far
jokes.punchline: Frank interprets 'heroin' as Nordberg requesting actual heroin as a pain drug — and promises to try to procure it
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the escalating misinterpretation sequence and one of the great ZAZ punchlines. After two beats of misinterpretation, the audience has the pattern — but 'Nordberg, that's a pretty tall order. Give me a couple of days on that one' is still a shock because of its casual delivery and the specific implication that Frank will actually try to GET him heroin. 'Give me a couple of days' is perfect economy — it implies Frank is mentally scheduling illegal drug procurement as a favor to a friend. This approaches the 9.5 craft anchor in construction.

jokes.text: "A gang of thugs, a blackmailer, an angry husband, a gay lover..."
jokes.setup: Wilma asks who would do such a thing to good, harmless Nordberg
jokes.punchline: Frank's list of suspects casually escalates from plausible (gang of thugs) to increasingly suggestive of Nordberg's secret life (angry husband, gay lover), all delivered without inflection
jokes.explanation: A list joke that works through escalation and frank obliviousness. The rhythm builds from generic to specific to embarrassingly personal, with Frank apparently unaware he's just implied Nordberg had a secret life to Nordberg's wife. Good character integration — only Drebin would say this.

jokes.text: "A parachute not opening — that's the way to die, getting caught in a combine, having your nuts bit off by a Laplander. That's the way I want to go."
jokes.setup: Ed says 'no way for a man to die' about Nordberg being shot; Frank appears to agree
jokes.punchline: Frank's agreement transforms into an increasingly specific and bizarre list of deaths he would prefer — culminating in 'having your nuts bit off by a Laplander'
jokes.explanation: One of the most memorable lines in ZAZ's filmography and the best pure joke in this reel. The setup (agreeing with Ed) makes Frank sound reasonable for one beat, before the list of increasingly disturbing and specific preferred deaths takes over. 'Having your nuts bit off by a Laplander' is such a specific, geographically inexplicable, physically horrifying image delivered with total serenity that it's genuinely shocking and hilarious simultaneously. Approaches the 9.5 anchor — it's odd it isn't more culturally quotable given its quality.

jokes.text: "He's right, Wilma, but don't wait till the last minute to fill out those organ donor cards."
jokes.setup: Frank has just reassured Wilma that Nordberg will be okay and to think positive
jokes.punchline: Ed immediately undercuts this with practical advice to fill out organ donor cards — implying he doesn't share Frank's optimism
jokes.explanation: Clean, well-timed dark comedy. The juxtaposition of Frank's forced optimism with Ed's pragmatic death-preparation advice is sharp. 'Don't wait till the last minute' implies they're already past the point of optimism. Good economy.

jokes.text: "He's welcome back at Police Squad. Unless he's a drooling vegetable, but that's only common sense."
jokes.setup: Frank reassures Wilma that Nordberg's job will be waiting for him when he recovers
jokes.punchline: He adds the exception clause — 'unless he's a drooling vegetable' — as if this is simply a reasonable administrative policy, not a devastating thing to say to someone's wife
jokes.explanation: 'But that's only common sense' is the key — it frames a horrifying HR policy as reasonable workplace management. This is classic Drebin: sincerely trying to be kind while being devastatingly oblivious. Character integration is excellent.

jokes.text: "A photograph! 'I Luv You' out of Caracas. A Panamanian ship." / "When he said 'I love you,' he was telling you the name of the ship!" / "I realise that... now."
jokes.setup: Wilma produces a photograph of a ship named 'I Luv You'; Frank makes the connection to Nordberg's hospital words
jokes.punchline: Wilma's flat 'I realise that... now' — the callback to Joke #11 — reveals she was sitting on the answer the whole time while Frank was returning the sentiment
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback that retroactively makes the earlier joke even funnier. Wilma's weary 'I realise that... now' is both funny and character-revealing — she watched Frank earnestly return 'I love you' to her dying husband without understanding the context. Good structural use of the callback format.

jokes.text: "Wilma, whatever scum did this, no man will rest until he's behind bars. Let's grab a bite to eat."
jokes.setup: Frank makes a solemn, dramatic vow to bring justice for Nordberg to his tearful wife
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots — in the same breath — to asking if anyone wants to grab food
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic deflation in the ZAZ mold. The juxtaposition — dramatic oath followed instantly by 'let's grab a bite' — works through the absolute commitment of the transition. No pause, no recognition. This is one of the cleaner examples of Drebin's obliviousness-as-comedy in this reel.

jokes.text: "Louder!" — Frank's microphone moment at the press conference; he is told to speak louder and given a radio mic
jokes.setup: Frank begins his official speech at the Queen's visit press conference
jokes.punchline: He's apparently been speaking into a dead or inadequate mic; the correction via radio mic leads into the next joke
jokes.explanation: Setup beat for a larger visual gag sequence. Modest on its own but serves the escalating press conference comedy.

jokes.text: "No matter how silly the idea of having a queen might be to us, as Americans we must be gracious and considerate hosts."
jokes.setup: Frank is delivering an official diplomatic speech about the Queen's visit on behalf of the Police Department
jokes.punchline: He editorializes mid-speech about how silly the concept of monarchy is — directly undermining the entire purpose of the event
jokes.explanation: Drebin delivering a diplomatic speech while casually insulting the monarchy to their faces (and to the press) is a perfect character moment. The qualifier 'as Americans we must be gracious' tries to paper over the insult while making it worse. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Extended visual gag: Frank's radio mic is picking up signals — apparently broadcasting other audio (police scanner, music, etc.) — while dignitaries on stage react with increasing discomfort as Frank continues speaking obliviously
jokes.setup: Frank has been given a radio microphone to amplify his speech; it broadcasts normally at first
jokes.punchline: The mic begins picking up stray transmissions/sounds, increasingly embarrassing content broadcasts to the entire room while Frank continues his speech without noticing
jokes.explanation: A sustained visual gag that works through escalation and Drebin's complete imperviousness to the chaos he's causing. The transcript shows the dignitaries losing composure progressively while Frank continues ('Indeed, it is for all the people... Especially exciting...') — classic ZAZ visual comedy. Difficult to fully score from transcript alone but clearly a major set piece.

jokes.text: "Do you wanna take a dinghy?" / "No, I took care of that at the press conference."
jokes.setup: Ed asks if Frank wants to take a small boat (dinghy) out to where Nordberg was found
jokes.punchline: Frank mishears or reinterprets 'dinghy' as a bodily function/embarrassment, implying he already relieved himself or was embarrassed at the press conference
jokes.explanation: A compact wordplay/callback hybrid. 'Dinghy' sounds like 'dingy' or is interpreted as a crude euphemism; the callback to the press conference disaster ('I took care of that') implies Frank did something embarrassing there. Works in two directions simultaneously and is well-timed. Good economy.

jokes.text: Extended bribery exchange at the harbour: Frank and the harbourmaster exchange bills in an escalating negotiation, each offering larger sums to get/withhold information, with neither side appearing to have enough
jokes.setup: Frank flashes money ('maybe this'll refresh your memory') in a standard cop-movie informant shakedown
jokes.punchline: The exchange escalates into an absurd back-and-forth where both men are paying each other, neither can get what they want, and the harbourmaster asks Frank to spot him a 20
jokes.explanation: A clever subversion of the standard film noir bribery scene. By having both parties pay and counter-pay, ZAZ reveals the transaction as pure ritual rather than useful exchange. The ask 'can you spot me a 20?' at the end perfectly deflates both characters. The routine escalation structure is well-executed.

jokes.text: "Lieutenant." / "The feeling is mutual. Nice to meet you, too. Cuban?" / "No, Dutch-Irish. My father was from Wales."
jokes.setup: Ludwig greets Frank professionally; Frank appears to respond in kind before Ludwig offers a cigar ('Cuban?')
jokes.punchline: Frank interprets 'Cuban?' (referring to the cigar) as a question about his ethnic background and answers accordingly — including the non-sequitur 'my father was from Wales'
jokes.explanation: Classic ZAZ misunderstanding gag with an extra comedic layer: 'Dutch-Irish. My father was from Wales' answers a question that wasn't asked while being internally inconsistent (Dutch-Irish but from Wales). The willingness to give a full biographical answer to what was clearly a cigar offer is pitch-perfect Drebin obliviousness. Good economy.

jokes.text: Ludwig's elaborate description of his priceless Samurai pen — 'a gift from Emperor Hirohito, unbreakable, impervious to everything but water' — as Frank presumably destroys it
jokes.setup: Ludwig lovingly describes each priceless object in his office, building the value and irreplaceability of his Samurai pen
jokes.punchline: The elaborate setup ('impervious to everything but water') is immediately paid off when Frank — through oblivious bumbling — presumably exposes it to water or breaks it
jokes.explanation: A Chekhov's gun joke done comedically: Ludwig telegraphs the weakness ('impervious to everything but water') and the audience knows Drebin will trigger it. The structure is clean and the execution is reliable. The setup's specificity ('gift from Emperor Hirohito') raises the stakes of the eventual destruction nicely.

jokes.text: "He's in the intensive care ward at Our Lady of the Worthless Miracle."
jokes.setup: Frank tells Ludwig which hospital Nordberg is in
jokes.punchline: The hospital is named 'Our Lady of the Worthless Miracle' — a fake Catholic hospital name that implies the miracles performed there are known to be mediocre
jokes.explanation: Brilliant throwaway name gag. 'Our Lady of the Worthless Miracle' is comedy writing at the word-choice level — 'worthless miracle' is an oxymoron that implies the hospital's miracles are real but specifically unhelpful. Maximum impact per word. This is the kind of gag ZAZ excels at: a fake proper noun that's funnier than any setup-punchline could achieve in the same space.

jokes.text: "Do you have any idea what was out there just five years ago?" / [pause] / "You bet you do. Orange groves!"
jokes.setup: Ludwig asks Frank a rhetorical question about the land his development sits on, expecting Frank to admit he doesn't know
jokes.punchline: Ludwig's instant self-correction — 'You bet you do. Orange groves!' — implies Frank somehow guessed or said the answer, treating him as a knowledgeable partner in a monologue
jokes.explanation: A mild misdirection joke. The rhetorical question format is subverted when Ludwig answers his own question enthusiastically as if Frank responded correctly. Functional but not among the reel's stronger gags.

jokes.text: "Are you all right, Lieutenant? Let me get you some Kleenex." — Ludwig pauses his villain monologue to tend to Frank
jokes.setup: Frank has apparently knocked something over or done something embarrassing/messy in Ludwig's office while Ludwig was delivering his grand monologue
jokes.punchline: Ludwig, mid-villain speech, has to stop and offer Kleenex like a concerned host
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of villain grandiosity and the mundane Kleenex offer works as a beat in the sustained office destruction sequence. Modest in isolation but serves the escalating comedy of the scene.

jokes.text: "Well, he hasn't been able to tell us a thing so far, but as soon as he regains consciousness, we'll see if he can still play the guitar."
jokes.setup: Ludwig asks if Nordberg has told Frank anything useful about the crime
jokes.punchline: Frank's response about waiting to see if Nordberg 'can still play the guitar' is a completely disconnected non-sequitur — nobody mentioned guitar, it has no bearing on the investigation
jokes.explanation: Pure Drebin absurdism. The guitar non-sequitur is completely unmotivated by context, suggesting Frank has entire private concerns about Nordberg's musical recovery that have nothing to do with the case. What elevates it is the confidence of delivery — it sounds like a reasonable follow-up thought. Good economy and strong character integration.

jokes.text: Frank meets Jane Spencer — extended comedic reaction beat as Frank is overwhelmed by attraction, presumably accompanied by exaggerated music, slow motion, or similar visual treatment
jokes.setup: Frank is in the middle of a professional police investigation at a suspect's office
jokes.punchline: He sees Jane and completely loses all composure and investigative purpose; the entire scene grinds to a halt as he is visibly smitten
jokes.explanation: A romantic comedy trope played for laughs through Drebin's complete professionalism abandonment. Works better on screen with the visual/musical treatment. The transcript captures the effect ('Oh!') but most of the comedy is visual. Scores modestly as a transcript entry — clearly more effective viewed.

jokes.text: Frank Drebin noir voiceover: 'Her hair was the colour of gold in old paintings. She had a full set of curves and the kind of legs you'd like to suck on for a day.'
jokes.setup: Classic hardboiled detective noir voiceover describing a femme fatale — 'full set of curves' is standard pulp fiction language
jokes.punchline: 'The kind of legs you'd like to suck on for a day' — derails the elegant simile with an absurdly literal, vaguely obscene image delivered in the same deadpan tone
jokes.explanation: Exceptional example of ZAZ's core technique: set up a recognizable genre convention (noir narration), lull the audience with the expected rhythm, then detonate it with a phrase that is both too literal and too absurd. 'Suck on for a day' is committed to the same deadpan register as the rest, which makes it funnier than if it were winking. High character integration because Drebin's oblivious sincerity is the whole joke. Scores 8+ because it's a genuinely sharp piece of genre parody writing, not merely a cheap non-sequitur.

jokes.text: Drebin voiceover: 'She gave me a look I could feel in my hip pocket.'
jokes.setup: Continuation of the noir voiceover style — 'a look I could feel' is a classic hardboiled simile
jokes.punchline: 'In my hip pocket' — bathetically locates the charged romantic feeling in the least romantic body part, undercutting the poetry
jokes.explanation: A solid, economical piece of noir-deflation humor. Less explosive than the leg-sucking line before it, but it maintains the rhythm. The bathos is well-executed — 'hip pocket' instead of 'spine' or 'chest' grounds the romance absurdly. Functional professional comedy writing.

jokes.text: Frank enters Jane's office; a taxidermied beaver is mounted on the wall. Frank: 'Nice beaver.' Jane: 'Thank you. I just had it stuffed.'
jokes.setup: Frank sincerely compliments what appears to be a double entendre — the audience hears a crude compliment to Jane herself
jokes.punchline: Jane holds up/gestures to the actual taxidermied beaver on the wall, and her response 'I just had it stuffed' is perfectly innocent yet compounds the innuendo
jokes.explanation: One of the most celebrated jokes in the entire film and in the ZAZ canon. Perfect double-entendre construction: Drebin is 100% sincere (he literally sees a beaver), Jane is 100% innocent (she's talking about taxidermy), yet every word functions simultaneously on the crude level. 'I just had it stuffed' is the killer second beat — it cannot be improved. The visual reveal makes the joke three-dimensional. Economy is flawless: five words of setup, four words of punchline, zero wasted syllables. This is the benchmark 9.5/10 joke for this reel.

jokes.text: Frank immediately: 'Let me help you with that.' — offering to help Jane carry the stuffed beaver down from the wall
jokes.setup: The double-entendre of the beaver joke has just landed; any continuation risks over-explaining
jokes.punchline: Frank's offer is innocent (he's helping carry the mount) but continues the innuendo perfectly, escalating rather than deflating the gag
jokes.explanation: The ideal button to the beaver joke — ZAZ knows not to let the best joke in the scene end on Jane's line. Frank's offer to 'help with that' extends the double-meaning by exactly one beat before moving on. It earns its 8+ because it demonstrates restraint AND escalation simultaneously: one more layer of innuendo, then out. Many comedies would over-explain here; this doesn't.

jokes.text: Jane: 'I've heard police work is dangerous.' Frank: 'Yes, that's why I carry a big gun.' Jane: 'Couldn't it go off accidentally?' Frank: 'I used to have that problem.' Jane: 'What did you do about it?' Frank: 'I just think about baseball.'
jokes.setup: Ostensibly a conversation about the dangers of carrying a firearm as a police officer
jokes.punchline: The exchange maps perfectly onto premature ejaculation — Frank's remedies ('think about baseball') are the classic advice for that problem, delivered with complete sincerity about his gun
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in sustained double-entendre construction. Each Q&A beat works on both literal levels simultaneously and the escalation is perfectly paced: 'big gun' → 'go off accidentally' → 'used to have that problem' → 'think about baseball.' The final line lands as the punchline because 'thinking about baseball' is culturally recognized specifically as an anti-arousal technique. Drebin never winks; he is fully committed to talking about his sidearm. This is among the best-crafted joke sequences in the reel.

jokes.text: Frank: 'That's a honey of an ankle-bracelet you have there.' Jane: 'Did it slip down there again?'
jokes.setup: Frank pays what seems like a flirtatious compliment to something on Jane's lower leg
jokes.punchline: Jane's response implies the bracelet has slipped from somewhere higher — suggesting it's actually a garter, transforming Frank's sincere observation into inadvertent flirtation
jokes.explanation: A lighter version of the double-entendre pattern established in the previous jokes. Works well because Jane's response does the heavy lifting — 'did it slip down there again?' is a great line. Slightly lower than the gun sequence because the mapping is less precisely constructed and the punchline less specific.

jokes.text: Frank: 'How about dinner? I know a place that serves great Viking food.'
jokes.setup: Frank tries to charm Jane into a date — a standard romantic moment
jokes.punchline: 'I know a place that serves great Viking food' — Viking food is a completely inexplicable, non-romantic choice that reveals Frank's social obliviousness
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures Frank Drebin's character through a single non-sequitur: he is trying to be romantic and smooth, and 'Viking food' is what he comes up with. The specificity of 'Viking' (not just 'Nordic' or 'Scandinavian') makes it funnier — it implies medieval mead halls, not a nice dinner. High character integration because only Frank Drebin would make this his best romantic move. Earns 8+ because the absurdity is precisely calibrated and completely character-revealing.

jokes.text: Jane declines dinner, citing that 'tomorrow being Arbor Day.'
jokes.setup: Jane needs a reason to decline Frank's dinner invitation — the audience expects a romantic obstacle or polite excuse
jokes.punchline: She cites Arbor Day — a minor, tree-planting holiday of no personal significance to anyone — as though it requires a full day of rest
jokes.explanation: Classic ZAZ bathos: the excuse is delivered with complete sincerity and yet is the most trivial possible reason imaginable. 'Arbor Day' as a reason to rest is a genuinely inspired choice — Thanksgiving or Christmas would be too understandable, 'I'm tired' too normal. Arbor Day is obscure enough to be absurd but recognizable enough that the audience knows it's not a real excuse. Economy is impeccable: two words do all the work.

jokes.text: Frank: 'How about a rain check?' Jane: 'Let's just stick to dinner.'
jokes.setup: Frank offers a 'rain check' as a polite alternative to the deferred dinner plan
jokes.punchline: Jane corrects him — 'rain check' means a future dinner, which is what he wanted; she redirects to sticking to dinner, as though he offered something different
jokes.explanation: A quick, competent verbal gag — Jane treats 'rain check' as an alternative to dinner rather than a form of it. It's a light wordplay beat that plays on the idiomatic meaning of the phrase. Works but is one of the thinner jokes in this sequence; it's a brief chuckle between larger gags.

jokes.text: Ted and Ed demonstrate an 'anti-graffiti wall' in the police lab — the wall physically retaliates against spray-painting vandals with mechanical violence when sensors are triggered.
jokes.setup: Frank visits the police lab expecting forensic results; instead finds the scientists occupied with an elaborate demonstration
jokes.punchline: The 'anti-graffiti wall' is a Rube Goldberg contraption that violently punishes taggers in real time — an absurdly over-engineered solution played completely straight
jokes.explanation: Classic ZAZ Q-branch parody — the police scientists are always working on gadgets that are both useless to Frank and spectacularly over-engineered for their stated purpose. The anti-graffiti wall is a good visual setpiece. The 'mazel tov!' from Frank is a funny button. Works as world-building comedy.

jokes.text: Frank reacts to the anti-graffiti wall demonstration: 'You've done it again — mazel tov!'
jokes.setup: Frank is watching an elaborate gadget demonstration
jokes.punchline: 'Mazel tov!' — a Yiddish congratulation Frank delivers with complete sincerity to his scientists, as if praising a bar mitzvah rather than a law-enforcement weapon
jokes.explanation: A quick, funny non-sequitur that characterizes Frank as someone who deploys vaguely inappropriate vocabulary with sincerity. The specific choice of 'mazel tov' implies the scientists are Jewish (a mild background gag) and that Frank sees their work as a celebration. Light but charming.

jokes.text: Ed and Ted present 'The Swiss Army Shoe' — an ordinary-looking shoe that conceals weapons, tools, and 'everything a cop would need'
jokes.setup: Riffing on the Swiss Army knife, the scientists present a shoe with hidden features — the audience expects gadget-movie parody
jokes.punchline: The concept itself is the joke: a shoe as the platform for a multi-tool, presented with complete earnestness as a practical police innovation
jokes.explanation: A reliable ZAZ gadget gag — the Swiss Army Shoe is an immediately legible parody of Bond/spy gadget movies. The humor comes from the visual absurdity of a heavily-armed shoe and the deadpan presentation. Solid mid-tier comedy moment in the lab sequence.

jokes.text: Ted demonstrates cufflink darts that knock out victims 'for a few minutes' — then immediately fires one at Ed, who collapses. Ted: 'Why?' (to himself, as if confused by his own action)
jokes.setup: Ted explains the cufflinks are dart guns and says 'Let me demonstrate on Ed' — the audience expects a staged, controlled demo
jokes.punchline: He shoots Ed, Ed drops; Ted's bewildered 'Ted! Why?' reaction suggests he surprised even himself, and 'Don't worry, he'll be up in no time' is delivered with casual disregard for his colleague
jokes.explanation: The snap physicality of the gag — Ted shooting his own partner mid-sentence — is very ZAZ. The 'Ted! Why?' line (spoken by Ted about himself, or possibly Ed before collapsing — the script implies self-reflexive bewilderment) is a funny button. The casual 'Don't worry, he'll be up in no time' normalizes the violence perfectly.

jokes.text: Al enters and Frank offers to fix something on his face — 'There's something on the side of your mouth, Al. No, no. The other side.' — Al keeps turning the wrong way.
jokes.setup: Frank tries to help Al clean his face; a simple, friendly interaction
jokes.punchline: Al keeps presenting the wrong side, extending the trivial moment into absurd territory through repeated failure — the visual of a cop unable to identify his own mouth sides
jokes.explanation: A light physical gag, functional but not exceptional. It's the kind of brief, throwaway bit ZAZ uses to fill transitions. The humor is in the awkwardness of a grown man unable to find his own mouth-side. Mid-tier.

jokes.text: Frank tries to look through a microscope with his eye closed; scientist tells him: 'Use your open eye, Frank.'
jokes.setup: Frank is shown evidence through a microscope — a standard lab scene
jokes.punchline: He uses the wrong eye (closed one), requiring the scientist to tell a grown police lieutenant to use his open eye — a humiliation delivered deadpan
jokes.explanation: Deceptively simple visual comedy that works because Leslie Nielsen plays it with complete commitment. The instruction 'use your open eye' is so basic it loops back around to being funny. Good character integration — this is exactly the sort of routine incompetence that defines Drebin.

jokes.text: Ludwig: 'Tell me, Mr Pahpshmir, in all the world, who is the most effective assassin?' Pahpshmir: 'I would think anyone who manages to conceal his identity as an assassin.' Ludwig: '...One who doesn't know he is an assassin.'
jokes.setup: Villain exposition scene — Ludwig is explaining his hypnosis plan
jokes.punchline: The concept of 'an assassin who doesn't know he is an assassin' is both a genuinely clever plot point AND an inherently absurd idea delivered with Bond-villain gravity
jokes.explanation: More of a plot-comedy hybrid — the idea is genuinely funny in its self-conscious villain-monologue pomposity, parodying the Bond villain who explains too much. The escalating pedantry ('Yes, but there is even a MORE ideal assassin') is the comedic texture.

jokes.text: The 'hypnotized assassin' sequence: Jane (under hypnosis) is ordered 'I must kill Pahpshmir' — she calmly serves tea, picks up and sets down a gun on the floor, then continues serving. Ludwig's butler notes 'There's a gun on the floor, sir!' Ludwig: 'Just leave it. It's all right.'
jokes.setup: Ludwig has revealed the concept of a hypnotic assassin who doesn't know they're an assassin; Jane enters to serve tea
jokes.punchline: Jane picks up a gun mid-tea-service, the butler announces it matter-of-factly as a minor domestic irregularity, Ludwig waves it off — the violent threat treated as a trivial inconvenience in proper British-butler fashion
jokes.explanation: The butler's announcement of a gun on the floor in the same register as 'you have a spot on your tie' is excellent deadpan comedy. Ludwig's breezy 'Just leave it, it's all right' is a perfect straight-man response that treats attempted assassination as a mild domestic inconvenience. The gap between the gravity of the situation and the casual response is the engine of the joke.

jokes.text: Ludwig, after demonstrating that Jane is a hypnotized assassin: 'Good secretaries are so hard to find these days.'
jokes.setup: Ludwig has just demonstrated to Pahpshmir that Jane is a programmed killer who doesn't know it
jokes.punchline: He pivots to lamenting the difficulty of finding good secretarial staff — treating her value as an assassin as equivalent to her value as an office worker
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in this reel. The joke works on multiple levels: (1) it treats assassination as a job perk, (2) it reduces Jane to her secretary role in the same breath as revealing her as a deadly weapon, (3) the pompous villain's mundane complaint undercuts any menace he might have. 'Good secretaries are so hard to find' is both a recognizable social cliché AND a genuinely dark observation about valuing a mind-controlled killer primarily for her filing skills. Earns 8+ because it's both funny and illuminating of Ludwig's character.

jokes.text: Drebin voiceover: 'I had 24 hours to find something to clear my friend's name... I returned to the hospital with Ludwig's records to try to jog Nordberg's memory.'
jokes.setup: Drebin's voiceover sets up his plan: use Ludwig's records to 'jog Nordberg's memory'
jokes.punchline: Nordberg is in a coma — he cannot be 'jogged' in any meaningful way. The plan is revealed as either absurd optimism or Drebin's fundamental incomprehension of medical states
jokes.explanation: A quiet character-based joke in the voiceover: Frank's plan to jog a coma patient's memory via paperwork is entirely Drebin-logical. Not a big laugh but a consistent characterization beat.

jokes.text: The hypnotized assassin arrives at the hospital, muttering 'I must kill Nordberg. I must kill Nordberg.' — Frank bursts in: 'Drebin, Police Squad! Let go of that pillow!'
jokes.setup: Tense thriller moment — an assassin is in Nordberg's hospital room attempting to smother him with a pillow
jokes.punchline: Frank's battle cry is 'Let go of that pillow!' — a heroic cop identifying himself and charging in to save his partner from... a pillow. The mundane object deflates the thriller tension entirely.
jokes.explanation: Classic ZAZ deflation: a moment of genuine dramatic tension (assassination attempt) undercut by the absurd specificity of 'Let go of that pillow!' Frank's cop-announcement instinct firing about a pillow is both funny and perfectly in character. The specificity of 'that pillow' (rather than 'him' or 'that weapon') is what makes it work — he is categorizing a murder weapon as a piece of bedding.

jokes.text: After the hospital fight, Frank gives chase: 'Drebin, Police Squad! Follow that black car!' — but he is commandeering a driving-lesson car; the student driver Stephanie is behind the wheel.
jokes.setup: Frank needs to chase a fleeing assassin's car — the standard police thriller pursuit
jokes.punchline: The only available vehicle is a driving school car with a terrified learner driver; Frank must direct both the chase AND give driving instructions simultaneously
jokes.explanation: A great comic premise with strong structural integrity. The humor comes from the collision of two incompatible activities: high-stakes police pursuit and patient driving instruction. The concept alone generates sustained comedy through the ensuing sequence.

jokes.text: During the high-speed car chase, Frank is simultaneously giving Stephanie driving-lesson instructions: 'Check your mirror. Signal. Now pull into traffic. Try and ease off on the brake.'
jokes.setup: They are in a high-speed chase through city streets
jokes.punchline: Frank gives calm, by-the-book driving school instructions ('check your mirror, signal') as though this were a normal lesson, while hurtling through traffic
jokes.explanation: The sustained comedy of Frank delivering calm, polite driving instruction during a catastrophic car chase is very well-executed. Each instruction ('check your mirror,' 'signal,' 'ease off the brake') is a perfect slice of banality placed against chaos. The gap between register and reality is the whole joke, and it's sustained over multiple beats without wearing out. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: During the chase: Frank: 'I know a short cut. Turn left here!' — resulting in chaos and disaster
jokes.setup: Frank has a shortcut that will improve the chase
jokes.punchline: The 'shortcut' leads into mayhem — the confidence of 'I know a short cut' is the promise that the film immediately demolishes
jokes.explanation: A reliable but not exceptional gag — the confident shortcut that makes things worse is a classic comedy move. Works within the chase sequence as one beat among many but isn't particularly distinctive.

jokes.text: Frank coaching during the chase: 'Normally, you would not be going 65 down the wrong way of a one-way street.'
jokes.setup: They are going 65 mph the wrong way down a one-way street during a chase
jokes.punchline: Frank acknowledges the abnormality with a calm instructor's caveat ('normally you would not be...') as though this were a marginal deviation from standard lesson procedure
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the chase sequence. 'Normally, you would not be going 65 down the wrong way of a one-way street' is exquisitely phrased — the word 'normally' does enormous work, implying that this situation is an understandable exception while maintaining the instructor's equanimity. It's highly quotable and captures everything great about Drebin's deadpan persona.

jokes.text: Another driver, cut off by the chase car, leans out and shouts: 'You dumb broad!' at Stephanie. Frank: 'Stephanie...' then calmly instructs: 'Gently extend your arm. Extend your middle finger.'
jokes.setup: Stephanie is insulted by an aggressive driver; a moment of road-rage confrontation
jokes.punchline: Frank responds by giving an instructor's formal, step-by-step guide to flipping the bird — treating the rude gesture as a teachable driving-lesson skill delivered with complete pedagogical calm
jokes.explanation: Possibly the best single line in the car chase sequence and among the finest in the reel. 'Gently extend your arm. Extend your middle finger.' is a flawless piece of comedy writing: it takes something crude (flipping someone off) and elevates it through the clinical, instructor register of 'gently' and the step-by-step breakdown. The word 'gently' alone is worth a point. Frank endorsing the rude gesture — while maintaining pedagogical decorum — is perfect character comedy. Earns its high score.

jokes.text: After the middle-finger instruction, Frank enthuses: 'Very good. Well done.'
jokes.setup: Stephanie has just flipped off a driver per Frank's instruction
jokes.punchline: Frank praises her with the warm, encouraging words of a proud driving instructor — 'Very good. Well done.' — as though she parallel-parked successfully
jokes.explanation: Perfect button to the middle-finger gag. 'Very good. Well done.' in an approving instructor's tone is exactly right — it validates the obscene gesture as though it were a milestone achievement in Stephanie's driving education. Economy of four words doing maximum work.

jokes.text: After the chaotic car chase ends in destruction, Frank steps out and addresses bystanders: 'All right, move on! Nothing to see here! Please disperse! Nothing to see here. Please!'
jokes.setup: An enormous, spectacular crash has just occurred — an unmissable disaster clearly visible to everyone on the street
jokes.punchline: Frank earnestly orders people to disperse because there's 'nothing to see here,' standing in front of spectacular wreckage, speaking to a crowd that has everything to see
jokes.explanation: A reliable ZAZ irony beat — 'nothing to see here' in front of maximum chaos is a classic running joke in the Police Squad franchise. It's funny but familiar by this point in the series' history. The joke works through pure irony and Drebin's obliviousness, though it's not the freshest execution of the gag.

jokes.text: Drebin voiceover after the chase: 'The attempt on Nordberg's life left me shaken and disturbed. The questions kept coming up again and again, like bubbles in a case of soda.'
jokes.setup: Drebin sets up a noir-style reflection on the case; the audience expects a poetic simile
jokes.punchline: 'Like bubbles in a case of soda' — the simile is bathetically mundane, replacing the expected hard-boiled poetry ('like a leaky faucet I couldn't fix') with a grocery-store image
jokes.explanation: Another well-executed noir-deflation voiceover simile. 'Like bubbles in a case of soda' is a funny image because it's almost poetic but specifically domestic and unromantic. Consistent with the reel's established pattern of voiceover bathos, but slightly lower impact than the opening leg-sucking simile because the technique is now familiar.

jokes.text: Drebin voiceover: '...And where the hell was I?' — ending a list of questions about the case
jokes.setup: Frank's voiceover has been rattling off a series of investigative questions about the case ('Who was this character? Why was he trying to kill Nordberg? Did Ludwig lie to me?')
jokes.punchline: The final question is not about the case at all — it's Frank admitting he has lost track of his own train of thought mid-monologue
jokes.explanation: Genuinely delightful meta-character moment. The escalating series of detective questions builds an expectation of increasingly sharp investigative insight — and then Frank asks 'where the hell was I?' not as a philosophical question but as a sincere admission of confusion about his own monologue. It perfectly exposes Drebin's incompetence while maintaining his oblivious sincerity. High character integration and economy.

jokes.text: Jane has let herself into Frank's home and is making dinner; Frank arrives home to find her there. Jane: 'You're late.' Frank: 'That depends on what I'm late for.'
jokes.setup: Jane accuses Frank of being late; a mild social accusation with a clear expected response ('I'm sorry')
jokes.punchline: Frank's reply — 'That depends on what I'm late for' — refuses to accept the premise of lateness because he didn't know she was coming; the logic is correct but socially absurd
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-constructed piece of Drebin logic. His response is technically accurate — he can't be late for something he didn't know about — but delivered as a suave comeback, which makes his obliviousness charming rather than rude. Good character voice.

jokes.text: Jane: 'I'm boiling a roast.' Beat. Frank: 'How hot and wet do you like it?' Jane: 'Very hot and awfully wet.'
jokes.setup: Jane announces she's cooking; both characters are ostensibly discussing a boiled roast
jokes.punchline: The exchange about cooking temperature and moisture maps precisely onto sexual desire; both deliver their lines with complete culinary sincerity
jokes.explanation: Another well-constructed double-entendre in the ZAZ mode. 'Very hot and awfully wet' is a good punchline — the word 'awfully' adds unexpected specificity. The double-meaning is clear but not labored. Slightly less surprising than the beaver/gun sequences earlier because the dinner scene has established a romantic-double-entendre register.

jokes.text: Jane: 'You seem to know your way around a kitchen.' Frank: 'I'm just as handy in other rooms of the house.'
jokes.setup: Jane observes Frank's kitchen skills
jokes.punchline: Frank's reply implies sexual competence while ostensibly claiming general home-handiness — a smooth double-entendre delivered with Drebin's characteristic sincerity
jokes.explanation: A lighter double-entendre — 'handy in other rooms' works fine but is less precisely constructed than the boiling roast exchange. The pattern is now established enough that the audience is ahead of the joke.

jokes.text: Jane explains she's wearing Frank's shirt because she 'didn't want to get stained or wrinkled... at least, not yet.'
jokes.setup: Jane explains the innocent reason she borrowed Frank's shirt (to protect her clothes while cooking)
jokes.punchline: 'At least... not yet' — the pause before 'yet' transforms the innocent explanation into a promise of future staining/wrinkling from romantic activity
jokes.explanation: One of the cleaner double-entendres in the dinner scene. The ellipsis before 'yet' is doing significant structural work — it signals the pivot from innocent to suggestive without explanation. Economy is excellent: two words ('not yet') carry the entire punchline. The timing implied by '...at least, not yet' is what distinguishes this from the simpler double-entendres around it.

jokes.text: Jane: 'Do you mind if I slip into something more comfortable?' — she returns wearing a full suit of armor. Frank: 'There. That's better.'
jokes.setup: 'Do you mind if I slip into something more comfortable?' — one of cinema's most recognizable come-on lines, setting up the expectation of lingerie
jokes.punchline: Jane returns in a full suit of armor — the most maximally uncomfortable and unsexy possible garment — and Frank responds as though this is completely normal and welcome
jokes.explanation: One of the best visual gags in the reel and among the best in the film. The setup is a universally recognized cinematic cliché — 'slip into something more comfortable' has been used as a seduction line in thousands of movies. The audience has precisely one expectation. ZAZ subverts it with the most extreme possible opposite: medieval armor. Frank's approval ('There. That's better.') completes the joke by refusing to acknowledge the absurdity. Perfect structure, maximum economy, superb visual commitment. Earns high craft and impact scores.

jokes.text: While interrogating Jane over dinner about the unregistered ship, Frank asks about photographs from Ludwig's docks. Jane: 'I was young. I needed the work.'
jokes.setup: Frank mentions photographs he saw at Ludwig's docks — the audience (and Jane) initially interpret this as potentially compromising personal photos
jokes.punchline: Jane immediately goes into a defensive mode about being young and needing money — implying the photos are embarrassing/compromising — before Frank clarifies they're surveillance photos of a ship
jokes.explanation: A quick, clean misdirection gag: Jane's assumption that the photographs are personal/compromising generates her defensive confession ('I was young, I needed the work') before the correction. The joke implies a past Jane would rather not discuss, adding comic character depth. The economy of four words revealing an entire implied backstory is excellent.

jokes.text: Jane: 'How is your... meat?' — pause — Frank responds nonverbally with the audience seeing some physical reaction or expression.
jokes.setup: In the context of the romantically charged dinner with multiple double-entendres already established, Jane asks 'How is your... meat?' with a pointed pause before 'meat'
jokes.punchline: The pause turns a culinary question into an unmistakable sexual double-entendre; Frank's reaction and the visual of the food complete the gag
jokes.explanation: By this point in the dinner sequence, the double-entendre register is well established, so this is working more as a continuation of the pattern than a surprise. The ellipsis before 'meat' is a less elegant version of the 'not yet' construction. Functional but the thinnest of the dinner double-entendres.

jokes.text: Frank replies to 'How is your meat?' — he holds up multiple portions or makes a visual display: 'I've got nine more.'
jokes.setup: Jane's pointed meat question; the audience is awaiting Frank's response in the established double-entendre mode
jokes.punchline: 'I've got nine more' — on the literal level, Frank has ten cuts of meat; on the other level, the boast is absurdly comic in its specificity and obliviousness
jokes.explanation: The punchline 'I've got nine more' is better than expected — the specificity of 'nine' makes it funnier than 'several more' or 'plenty more' would be. It implies Frank has prepared a truly excessive amount of meat and is offering it with the same deadpan sincerity. The number is the joke.

jokes.text: Frank tastes the meat and responds: 'You be the judge of that.' — sliding the plate back or indicating she should taste it, followed by an impressed food-reaction that is clearly a sexual-satisfaction reaction
jokes.setup: Jane has asked how Frank's meat is; he has apparently tasted it
jokes.punchline: 'You be the judge of that' — an unusually deflecting response to a direct question about food quality, with the ambiguity of whether he's referring to the cooking or something else entirely
jokes.explanation: The weakest of the dinner innuendo gags. 'You be the judge of that' is vague enough to work as a double entendre but doesn't have a clear or surprising comedic mechanism. By this beat the double-entendre sequence has been running for three minutes and the novelty is depleted.

jokes.text: Frank: 'If it wasn't [violent], I'd be out of a job, but I'd give it up tomorrow to live in a world without crime.' Jane: 'That's beautiful.'
jokes.setup: Jane laments that the world is a violent place; Frank responds as a detective reflecting on his vocation
jokes.punchline: Frank's statement is simultaneously a cliché virtue-signal AND a genuine admission that his career depends on crime — Jane responds with sincere admiration to this logically contradictory sentiment
jokes.explanation: A quiet but effective piece of character comedy. Frank's logical contradiction — 'I'd give up my crime-dependent career to live in a crime-free world' — is treated as profound by Jane. Drebin's earnestness in saying something self-contradictory is in perfect character. Not a big laugh but a smart, dry moment.

jokes.text: Frank begins his sad romantic backstory about an ex-girlfriend who traveled with the 'Chicago Male Chorus and Symphony' 300 days a year — 'I don't recall her playing an instrument or being able to sing.'
jokes.setup: Frank shares a vulnerable romantic backstory — the kind of moment that in a straight drama would generate sympathy
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts any sympathy by noting she couldn't play music or sing, implying she was not, in fact, with a chorus — but Frank has somehow processed this as innocent
jokes.explanation: A great Drebin character-comedy moment: he is describing in clinical detail the evidence that his girlfriend was cheating on him with an entire symphony orchestra, without ever connecting the dots. His obliviousness to his own cuckolding is funny and also genuinely tender. High character integration because only Drebin could deliver this backstory with such guileless sincerity.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Yet she was on the road 300 days of the year. I bought her a harp for Christmas. She asked me what it was.'
jokes.setup: Frank is building the case that his girlfriend was away with the symphony/chorus despite having no musical ability
jokes.punchline: 'I bought her a harp for Christmas. She asked me what it was.' — the girlfriend didn't even recognize the instrument she supposedly traveled with professionally, confirming the infidelity to everyone except Frank
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the cheating-girlfriend backstory reaches its peak here. 'She asked me what it was' — referring to a harp — is a devastating detail that proves she had no connection to the orchestra and yet Frank still doesn't see it. The harp is the perfect choice: it's the most distinctive, recognizable, impractical instrument possible (a cellist might plausibly not know other instruments; a harp is unmistakable). The specificity elevates this to 8+. Drebin's delivery of this devastating detail with complete sadness rather than suspicion is perfect character comedy.

jokes.text: Frank: 'It's the same old story. Boy finds girl. Boy loses girl. Girl finds boy. Boy forgets girl. Boy remembers girl. Girl dies in a blimp accident over the Orange Bowl on New Year's Day.'
jokes.setup: Frank begins the familiar 'same old story' formula — 'boy meets girl, boy loses girl' — a cliché romantic narrative structure
jokes.punchline: The formula keeps extending with increasingly specific plot beats until it ends with 'girl dies in a blimp accident over the Orange Bowl on New Year's Day' — an absurdly specific, catastrophic, and sports-venue-specific death
jokes.explanation: One of the great comic escalations in the film. The technique is perfect: 'same old story' signals a brief cliché, but then it keeps going — 'girl finds boy, boy forgets girl, boy remembers girl' — each addition is funny because it's unexpected detail that builds absurd narrative complexity, and then the finale lands: 'girl dies in a blimp accident over the Orange Bowl on New Year's Day.' The specificity of 'blimp,' 'Orange Bowl,' and 'New Year's Day' is extraordinary — each word earns its place. The Orange Bowl (a football venue) on New Year's Day (when the Orange Bowl game is traditionally played) suggests Goodyear Blimp territory, making the subsequent Goodyear pun structurally set up. Among the best-constructed comic escalations in this reel.

jokes.text: After Frank mentions the blimp accident, Jane asks: 'Goodyear?' Frank: 'No, the worst.'
jokes.setup: Jane asks 'Goodyear?' — intending to ask whether it was a Goodyear blimp (the famous brand associated with the Orange Bowl)
jokes.punchline: Frank interprets 'Goodyear?' as 'Was it a good year?' and responds 'No, the worst' — a perfect double-meaning that works on both levels
jokes.explanation: The best single joke in this reel and one of the most beloved gags in the entire Naked Gun franchise. The structure is impeccable: (1) the blimp-at-Orange Bowl detail sets up Goodyear naturally, (2) Jane's question 'Goodyear?' is a reasonable factual inquiry about the blimp brand, (3) Frank's response 'No, the worst' treats it as an evaluation of the year — completing both meanings simultaneously. The punchline is exactly two words. It requires zero explanation. It is impossible to improve. Frank's sadness in delivery makes it simultaneously funny and genuinely pathetic. This is what a 9.5+ looks like — a joke that could be discussed in comedy writing seminars.

jokes.text: Frank reassures Jane: 'What's in the past doesn't matter anyway. Maybe... Maybe we're just two lonely souls who have found each other.'
jokes.setup: Jane tries to confess something important to Frank; Frank cuts her off with a romantic sentiment
jokes.punchline: The irony: Frank is preventing Jane from confessing that she's a spy/double agent, with a romantic speech about not needing to know her past. His sweetness directly enables her deception — a dramatic irony the audience appreciates
jokes.explanation: More of a plot/irony beat than a pure laugh moment — the humor comes from dramatic irony (we know what Jane was about to confess) rather than a crafted joke. Functional but not a standout comedic moment.

jokes.text: Jane: 'Frank, it's not that. Why did you have to be so wonderful?' — crying, pulling away from an intimate moment for a reason other than what Frank assumes
jokes.setup: Frank tries to stop Jane from confessing something ('No! No need to tell me anything'), she begins to cry
jokes.punchline: Frank assumes she's moved by their romantic connection; she's actually crying because she's been sent to spy on him by Ludwig — making her 'you're so wonderful' a lament of guilt, not romance
jokes.explanation: A dark-irony moment that works better on second viewing when the audience knows Jane's espionage mission. The comedy is in the dramatic irony — 'why did you have to be so wonderful' means the opposite of what Frank thinks. It's more of a rewatch joke than a first-time laugh. Moderate impact.

jokes.text: In the middle of a romantic moment, the phone rings and Frank picks it up: 'Funny-face!'
jokes.setup: An intimate romantic moment between Frank and Jane is interrupted by a phone call
jokes.punchline: Frank answers with 'Funny-face!' — a term of endearment implying he has an ongoing intimate relationship with the caller, puncturing the romantic moment with Jane
jokes.explanation: A quick, effective comic beat — the romantic moment interrupted by a phone call answered with 'Funny-face!' implying another woman. The timing makes it work. Not a complex construction but punchy and well-placed.

jokes.text: Frank: 'I want you to know... I practise safe sex.' Jane: 'So do I.'
jokes.setup: Frank makes a sincere, modern public-health disclosure about safe sex before the implied love scene
jokes.punchline: Jane's reply 'So do I' — delivered with a beat and a smile — recontextualizes her entire character: she is simultaneously a romantic lead AND a cool, modern woman who appreciates the disclosure; the exchange parodies the 1988 safe-sex PSA culture with complete deadpan
jokes.explanation: A sharp period-specific gag that also works timelessly. In 1988, 'safe sex' was an extremely charged cultural topic (AIDS crisis PSA era); Frank's earnest disclosure is funny because it's so direct, clinical, and incongruous with the romantic moment. Jane's mirroring response turns it into a mutual announcement that parodies both the PSA culture and movie romance conventions. Good economy and genuine wit.

jokes.text: Frank: 'I want you to know... I practise safe sex.' Jane: 'So do I.'
jokes.setup: Frank and Jane are about to be intimate — Frank offers a sincere, earnest health disclosure
jokes.punchline: The frank (pun intended) announcement of safe sex practices as a pre-intimacy formality, delivered with complete Drebin seriousness, and Jane's matching earnest reply — the bureaucratic handling of a romantic moment is the joke
jokes.explanation: A smart, well-calibrated joke for 1988 — the PSA-style declaration of safe sex practices as foreplay is both a topical reference and perfect Drebin character comedy. Only Frank Drebin would treat sexual disclosure as a formal procedural step with the same gravity as signing evidence into custody. 'So do I' as the matching response from Jane is the ideal straight-woman reply. High character integration, good economy.

jokes.text: You're not just saying it, because we exchanged bodily fluids?
jokes.setup: Jane tells Frank she means it when she says she had a wonderful day — a tender romantic moment.
jokes.punchline: Frank responds with clinical, unsexy language ('exchanged bodily fluids') where any normal person would say 'slept together' — deadpan deflation of a romantic scene.
jokes.explanation: Frank's robotic, clinical register in an intimate moment is perfectly in character. The humor comes from the gap between emotional context and bureaucratic language — a ZAZ staple. Slightly less punchy than the nightcap joke but still strong character comedy.

jokes.text: Can I interest you in a nightcap? — No, thanks, I don't wear them.
jokes.setup: Jane offers Frank a nightcap (a drink) as a romantic gesture after their date.
jokes.punchline: Frank takes 'nightcap' literally as a sleeping hat, deadpanning that he doesn't wear them — classic ZAZ misdirection through deliberate obtuseness.
jokes.explanation: Perfect ZAZ economy — four words do all the work. Frank's literal-minded obtuseness is the engine of his character, so the joke is completely character-integrated. The double meaning is classic but executed with ideal timing and no wasted syllables. Scores high because the punchline is instantly surprising yet perfectly logical for Drebin.

jokes.text: I know. You take a chance getting up in the morning, crossing the street or sticking your face in a fan.
jokes.setup: Ed warns Frank that breaking into Ludwig's office is 'taking a big chance.'
jokes.punchline: Frank agrees philosophically — then includes 'sticking your face in a fan' in his list of everyday risks, an absurd escalation that undercuts his own sage tone.
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best lines. The list starts plausibly ('getting up in the morning, crossing the street') and then detonates with 'sticking your face in a fan' — specific, visual, absurd, and completely unnecessary. Drebin delivers it with utter sincerity, which is the whole joke. High quotability; the specificity of the fan makes it memorable and original. Earns an 8+ because it exemplifies ZAZ's best technique: deadpan absurdism with perfect list structure.

jokes.text: Frank breaks into Ludwig's office and searches it — a long near-silent scene of physical comedy and slapstick inferred from context, culminating in 'Bingo!'
jokes.setup: Frank sneaks into Ludwig's office alone at night to find evidence.
jokes.punchline: The gap from 43:57 to 44:57 (a full minute with no dialogue) followed by a triumphant 'Bingo!' implies an extended slapstick sequence — ZAZ films are dense with prop comedy, pratfalls, and sight gags during such sequences.
jokes.explanation: Cannot score the specific gags without visuals, but the long silence-then-'Bingo!' structure is a known comedy beat. Scored conservatively as a placeholder for the physical comedy block; the rewatch bonus reflects that ZAZ office-break-in sequences typically contain multiple layered sight gags.

jokes.text: sexual assault with a concrete dildo?!
jokes.setup: The judge reads a list of charges against Frank — 'destroying property, arson...' — a standard legal laundry list.
jokes.punchline: The list escalates to 'sexual assault with a concrete dildo?!' — an absurd, specific, and maximally outrageous final charge that stops the judge cold.
jokes.explanation: Classic ZAZ escalation — the list of charges is a setup that the audience expects to end at 'arson,' and the specific, bizarrely material detail ('concrete') transforms something transgressive into pure absurdism. The adjective 'concrete' is what elevates this from cheap shock to genuine craft — it's so specific it circles back to funny. The judge's visible shock (implied by the '?!') adds a reaction beat. One of the reel's highest-impact moments.

jokes.text: That's ridiculous! Where is this 'evidence'? Well... it... burned in the f-fire.
jokes.setup: Frank confidently accuses Ludwig of plotting to assassinate the Queen, claiming to have evidence.
jokes.punchline: The evidence burned in the fire — the fire Frank presumably caused during the break-in, undercutting his entire case with shameful bathos.
jokes.explanation: The stammer ('f-fire') and the irony of Frank destroying his own evidence while committing the crime is well-structured situational comedy. The callback to the arson charge makes it land harder on rewatch. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: When I see five weirdos dressed in togas stabbing a guy in a park, I shoot the bastards. That's my policy.
jokes.setup: The judge warns Frank about past trouble, referencing 'last year.'
jokes.punchline: The judge — the authority figure — casually admits to shooting five actors in a Shakespeare production, framing it as reasonable policing and 'policy.'
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The comic inversion of authority — the judge doing something MORE egregiously violent and illegal than the defendant — is a ZAZ specialty. 'That's my policy' as a straight-faced self-justification is quotable and chilling. The escalation into '...you killed five actors!' / 'Good ones.' is a perfect button (see joke 8). Earns 8+ for quotability, structure, and the satirical bite at law-enforcement self-righteousness.

jokes.text: You killed five actors! — Good ones.
jokes.setup: Frank points out that the judge killed five actors in a Shakespeare production.
jokes.punchline: The judge's only response is 'Good ones' — not a denial or justification, but a proud quality assessment of the actors he killed.
jokes.explanation: Two words. Perfect. 'Good ones' takes the judge's sociopathic indifference and adds an unexpected dimension — he's not remorseful, he's vaguely proud that he at least shot quality talent. The economy is flawless. The dark subversion is complete. This is the kind of two-word punchline that makes comedy writers weep with envy. Comparable in craft to the best ZAZ gags ever committed to film. Easily the strongest joke in this reel.

jokes.text: Are Woo back in business? They closed down three years ago. / Gee, has it been that long? I don't feel like Chinese tonight anyway.
jokes.setup: Frank and Jane are having a tense, emotionally charged argument about whether to trust Ludwig.
jokes.punchline: In the middle of the serious conversation, they suddenly discuss a Chinese restaurant ('Woo') that Frank apparently called; then just as suddenly return to the serious topic — the total non-sequitur is played as though it's completely normal.
jokes.explanation: Classic ZAZ mid-scene non-sequitur: a completely unrelated phone call or action interrupts the dramatic tension without acknowledgment. The restaurant digression and instant return to the serious argument is disorienting in the best way. Implies Frank placed a food order mid-confrontation. Strong originality score for the technique.

jokes.text: I'm sorry, I can't hear you! — Don't fire the gun while you're talking.
jokes.setup: Frank and a henchman are exchanging gunfire at the stockyards — a life-or-death confrontation.
jokes.punchline: Frank's complaint about the noise from the gun being fired mid-conversation treats a gunfight like a minor conversational inconvenience — the total inversion of appropriate danger response.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Drebin: treating being shot at as a mild social faux pas, like someone chewing with their mouth open. The economy is excellent — 'Don't fire the gun while you're talking' is a polite correction that belongs in an etiquette manual, not a gunfight. Earns 8+ for character integration and economy.

jokes.text: Ed, he's got a picture of your wife! — Ethel!
jokes.setup: Frank and Ed are confronting a suspicious-looking man at the reception. The man protests 'I got rights!' and Frank asks 'Yeah? What about this?'
jokes.punchline: The damning 'evidence' Frank reveals is a photo of Ed's wife — not incriminating at all. Ed's horrified cry of 'Ethel!' suggests the real scandal is personal (perhaps she's cheating with this man), completely changing the stakes.
jokes.explanation: Excellent misdirection: the tension of a security confrontation suddenly collapses into a soap-opera marital subplot. Ed's one-word devastated cry 'Ethel!' is a great character beat. Well structured with the 'What about this?' buildup.

jokes.text: All right, anyone else here seeing his wife?
jokes.setup: Ed is devastated that someone has a photo of his wife (implying an affair). The serious royal-security mission has just been derailed.
jokes.punchline: Frank turns to the crowd and treats the marital infidelity as a security sweep — polling the room for other men seeing Ed's wife, with total professional deadpan.
jokes.explanation: Extends the Ethel gag with Frank's signature inability to distinguish professional and personal crises. The image of a detective polling a formal reception for his partner's wife's lovers is absurdly funny. Great economy.

jokes.text: The gloves are off, I'm playing hardball. It's fourth and fifteen, and you're looking at a full court press.
jokes.setup: Frank confronts Ludwig at the reception, trying to deliver a threatening declaration.
jokes.punchline: Frank's tough-guy speech mixes metaphors from boxing, baseball, and basketball into incoherent sports-idiom soup — all delivered with complete conviction.
jokes.explanation: Classic ZAZ mixed-metaphor joke. The escalation of sport-idiom confusion is funny but slightly too long — by 'full court press' the audience has already clocked the joke. Still strong character comedy for Drebin's oblivious confidence.

jokes.text: A meeting that turned into a peek-a-boo session with bullets, set up by someone who's been playing me like a violin.
jokes.setup: Frank confronts Jane about the stockyard ambush.
jokes.punchline: Frank describes the gunfight as a 'peek-a-boo session with bullets' — a child's game used to describe an assassination attempt.
jokes.explanation: Frank's noir-flavored hard-boiled language ('peek-a-boo session with bullets,' 'playing me like a violin') is delivered straight and is characteristically absurd. The juxtaposition of a children's game with lethal gunfire is the core ZAZ approach.

jokes.text: Thumb me another one, shuckie-lumps!
jokes.setup: Jane insists Ludwig told her Frank called off the stockyard meeting — an alibi Frank doesn't believe.
jokes.punchline: 'Thumb me another one, shuckie-lumps' — a completely made-up dismissive phrase combining the cadence of 'pull the other one' with an invented, ridiculous pet name.
jokes.explanation: The ZAZ technique of absurd invented slang is on full display. 'Shuckie-lumps' as a pet name during an accusation of betrayal is funny because of its tonal mismatch — it's affectionate nonsense delivered with contempt. High originality for the pure invention.

jokes.text: Cops and women don't mix. Like eating a spoonful of Drano. It'll clean you out, but it'll leave you hollow inside.
jokes.setup: Frank is delivering a hard-boiled speech about why he can't trust Jane — a parody of noir detective philosophy.
jokes.punchline: The analogy for his heartbreak is eating drain cleaner — the metaphor is absurdly literal (Drano cleans pipes / it'll clean you out) and then the second clause ('leave you hollow inside') plays the double meaning completely straight.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel and a ZAZ classic. The structure is a perfect mock-noir simile: it starts as a cliché ('cops and women don't mix'), then uses a genuinely dangerous household product as the analogy, and then extends the metaphor so logically ('it'll leave you hollow inside') that it becomes simultaneously absurd and poetic. This is the ZAZ 'Snip, snap' level of quotability — a line that lands as genuine wisdom before you notice it's about drinking drain cleaner. Earns 8+ comfortably.

jokes.text: Like make love to me? — Frank!
jokes.setup: Jane says 'I only did what I was told to do!' to defend herself against Frank's suspicion.
jokes.punchline: Frank explicitly asks if 'what she was told' included sleeping with him — a devastatingly blunt question that horrifies Jane ('Frank!') and the audience simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: Frank's total inability to soften an accusation is fully in character. The cringe is real — asking 'Like make love to me?' is so direct it's both funny and briefly uncomfortable. Jane's one-word 'Frank!' reaction beat seals it.

jokes.text: You can take this back. — Whose is that?
jokes.setup: Frank is dramatically returning something to Jane as he walks away — the audience assumes it's a gift or ring from their relationship.
jokes.punchline: Frank asks 'Whose is that?' — the item Jane hands back is not his, suggesting it belongs to someone else entirely, implying Frank has been holding onto a stranger's property or that there's a whole other layer of confusion.
jokes.explanation: A quick ZAZ misdirection — the dramatic 'take this back' gesture undercut by the revelation that neither party owns the object. Works better visually (we'd see the item); in transcript form it's slightly opaque but clearly a sight-gag beat.

jokes.text: By the way... I faked every orgasm.
jokes.setup: Frank delivers a classic hard-boiled goodbye to Jane after their breakup — tender and devastating. The scene is playing as genuine drama.
jokes.punchline: Frank's parting shot: 'By the way... I faked every orgasm.' — inverting the classic female trope with complete deadpan sincerity, as if this is crucial information Jane needs.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in this reel and arguably one of the best single jokes in the film. It works on every level: (1) It subverts the cliché 'woman fakes orgasms' with a gender inversion delivered by a stone-faced man. (2) The 'by the way' construction makes it sound like a housekeeping item Frank forgot to mention. (3) It shatters the tone of the genuinely-played romantic breakup scene. (4) It's completely in character — Frank is too literal and oblivious to understand why this is an odd thing to say. (5) Maximum economy: five words. This is a 9+ joke. Comparable to the best in the ZAZ canon.

jokes.text: It's disgusting the way they splash this stuff all over the newspapers! What is journalism coming to? / You're laying on top of the Queen with her legs wrapped around you and they call that news!
jokes.setup: Frank has apparently ended up in a compromising physical position with Queen Elizabeth (from the reception chaos). Ed is reading the newspaper coverage.
