jokes.punchline: The 'disgusting' outrage about journalism is revealed to be specifically about the image of Frank on top of the Queen — the moral indignation is about tabloid excess, not about Frank's actions themselves.
jokes.explanation: Classic delayed reveal — the outrage sounds like normal press criticism until we learn what the story actually IS. The image of Frank on top of the Queen with her legs wrapped around him being printed in newspapers is brilliantly absurd. The indignation misdirects perfectly.

jokes.text: Just think, the next time I shoot someone, I could be arrested.
jokes.setup: Ed says 'They can't kick you off the Force, it's not fair.' Frank philosophically accepts the unfairness of life.
jokes.punchline: Frank's concern is not being fired, but the future legal consequence of doing his job — 'the next time I shoot someone, I could be arrested.' Shooting people is so routine for Frank that legal accountability is the novel injustice.
jokes.explanation: Superb character joke. Frank treats shooting people as a professional routine — the injustice isn't that he shot people, it's that future shootings might have legal consequences. 100% character-specific to Drebin and the satirical view of police impunity. Earns 8+ for character integration and the dark satirical edge.

jokes.text: Hey, look at that! The missing evidence in the Kilner case! My God, he WAS innocent! / He went to the chair two years ago, Frank. / Well... what's the use?
jokes.setup: Frank is moping about being fired. He randomly notices something.
jokes.punchline: Frank finds exonerating evidence for someone who was executed two years ago — and his reaction is a brief existential shrug ('What's the use?') before moving on. A man's wrongful execution is treated as a minor bureaucratic inconvenience.
jokes.explanation: One of the darkest and best jokes in the reel. The structure is a compressed tragedy-comedy: discovery of innocence → it's too late → 'what's the use?' The speed of the exchange and Frank's instant resignation is what makes it land. This is ZAZ at its darkest — using wrongful execution as a throwaway gag. The 'What good are these damn awards and citations?' follow-up makes it even better. Earns 8+ for audacity and structural tightness.

jokes.text: Frank, that's not your desk!
jokes.setup: Frank is slumped dramatically at a desk, wallowing in self-pity after being fired.
jokes.punchline: Ed points out that Frank is sitting at the wrong desk — he's been dramatically monologuing at someone else's workstation. The existential despair is physically misplaced.
jokes.explanation: Quick visual sight-gag that punctures the melodrama. 'Frank, that's not your desk!' deflates the entire self-pity sequence with one practical observation. Works perfectly on its economy.

jokes.text: He likes East German men.
jokes.setup: Jane tries to convince Frank there was 'never anything between Vincent and me.' Frank asks 'What about you?' implying she might like Ludwig.
jokes.punchline: Jane's proof that there was nothing between her and Ludwig is that Ludwig is gay — and specifically attracted to 'East German men.' The specificity of 'East German' is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'East German men' is a classic ZAZ technique — the nationality is arbitrary and therefore funnier than just 'men.' Works well as an economical revelation. Slight ding for character integration since it's really about Ludwig, not about Drebin's specific character voice.

jokes.text: What about you? / I like cops. / All right! Yeah! / Settle down. Take it easy.
jokes.setup: Jane says 'I like cops' in response to Frank asking if she likes Ludwig. It's a sincere declaration of her preference/attraction.
jokes.punchline: Frank's partner Ed immediately cheers 'All right! Yeah!' as if personally validated — before Frank has to tell him to settle down. Ed's vicarious enthusiasm for Frank's romantic news is a great secondary character beat.
jokes.explanation: Ed's unprompted vicarious excitement is the best part — he treats Frank's romantic reconciliation like a sporting victory. 'Settle down. Take it easy.' from Frank is a perfect straight-man reversal (the man who just got the good news is calmer than his partner). Solid ensemble comedy.

jokes.text: I'm a very lucky woman. — So am I.
jokes.setup: Jane emotionally tells Frank 'I'm a very lucky woman' — a sincere romantic statement.
jokes.punchline: Frank responds 'So am I' — agreeing that he is also a very lucky woman. Classic Drebin obliviousness/non-sequitur delivered as genuine sentiment.
jokes.explanation: Four words that land perfectly. Frank's 'So am I' either means he agrees he's a lucky woman (oblivious) or he's so distracted he's just mirroring her sentence back. Either reading is funny and completely in character. Perfect economy — no word is wasted. Earns 8+ for structure and character integration.

jokes.text: Hello! I'm Curt Gowdy, along with Jim Palmer, Tim McCarver, Dick Vitale, Mel Allen, Dick Enberg and Dr Joyce Brothers.
jokes.setup: Standard sports broadcast introduction: an announcer introduces himself and his broadcast partner(s).
jokes.punchline: The list of co-commentators escalates absurdly to include six additional names including sports legends from wildly different sports AND a psychologist ('Dr Joyce Brothers') — the sheer excess and the incongruous inclusion of Joyce Brothers is the gag.
jokes.explanation: Classic ZAZ list escalation — the more names accumulate the funnier it gets, and the final 'Dr Joyce Brothers' (a TV psychologist, not a sportscaster) is the perfect absurdist button. Works on quantity and incongruity.

jokes.text: Over there — these seats are taken.
jokes.setup: Frank is supposed to be undercover and 'out of sight' at the baseball stadium per the Mayor's orders. The Queen has just been welcomed to great fanfare.
jokes.punchline: Frank's attempt to stay hidden manifests as mundanely telling other fans that seats are taken — he's managing the seating logistics of a baseball game while supposedly conducting a covert assassination-prevention operation.
jokes.explanation: The visual of Drebin undercover while performing the most quotidian fan behavior — seat-guarding — perfectly encapsulates his character. The mundane line ('these seats are taken') deployed in a life-or-death context is very ZAZ. Works best visually.

jokes.text: Why he not here now? I do not like to wait for him. / Mr Pallazzo, our head usher will be here in two minutes. Please wait. / He should be here now! / I'll send him right over. / I do not wait for him! He waits for me!
jokes.setup: An imperious man named Pallazzo is waiting to be escorted by the head usher — apparently a VIP.
jokes.punchline: Pallazzo's explosive self-importance over a head usher — not a dignitary, just an usher — escalates to 'I do not wait for him! He waits for ME!' The fury is completely disproportionate to the subject matter.
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for the Pallazzo/national anthem payoff. The diva behavior over a head usher is funny but functions more as misdirection setup than standalone comedy. Scores lower as an isolated joke; its value is primarily structural.

jokes.text: Mr Pallazzo? I am the head usher. I am here to... Excuse me. / Mr Pallazzo? Yes? / I am the head usher. / One second.
jokes.setup: Frank has disguised himself as the head usher to get close to Pallazzo (who is apparently Ludwig's assassin). He approaches to introduce himself.
jokes.punchline: Frank's attempt to introduce himself to Pallazzo is interrupted repeatedly — either by Frank himself ('Excuse me') or by Pallazzo ('One second') — the introduction keeps failing. The spy thriller trope of the perfect cover is undercut by an inability to complete a sentence.
jokes.explanation: The repeated failed introduction is a physical/dialogue running gag that builds to the reveal of Frank singing the anthem. Good structural setup; moderate joke value on its own.

jokes.text: Ladies and gentlemen, please welcome internationally-renowned opera star, Enrico Pallazzo! / [Frank Drebin takes the microphone to sing the national anthem]
jokes.setup: Frank has disguised himself as the head usher to infiltrate the baseball game. We expect a covert spy operation. The stadium announcer introduces 'internationally-renowned opera star Enrico Pallazzo.'
jokes.punchline: Frank steps up to sing the national anthem — he IS Enrico Pallazzo (his cover identity), and the joke's full payoff (occurring just past this transcript's end) will be Frank singing the anthem terribly. The reveal that the covert operation involves Frank performing publicly for 60,000 people is the inversion.
jokes.explanation: One of the great slow-build setups in comedy film. The entire reel has been building toward Frank needing to infiltrate the game; the reveal that his 'covert' approach involves standing in front of 60,000 people as an opera star is a spectacular inversion. The transcript ends just at the moment of maximum setup tension. High structure and earned scores because this has been built across the whole reel. The payoff (singing) is presumably in the next reel but the setup moment here deserves full credit.

jokes.text: Frank Drebin, dressed as an umpire, asks a player if his bat is 'official' — clearly using a strip-search pretext to pat down players for the assassin
jokes.setup: Frank has gone undercover as a home plate umpire to search the baseball players for the killer; asking about the bat sounds like a legit umpire question
jokes.punchline: The question is a ruse — Frank is running his hands over the player as if inspecting the bat but is really frisking him, conflating police procedure with umpiring
jokes.explanation: Classic ZAZ misdirection — the line sounds mundane and umpire-appropriate but it's the first beat of an extended gag where Frank frisks players under the guise of officiating. Strong character integration because only Drebin would think this is a viable undercover technique.

jokes.text: The Angel Vision scoreboard shows 'unusual moments in baseball over the years' — the footage that plays is absurdist and comedic (implied by the long pause 65:05 and crowd reaction)
jokes.setup: Announcer introduces Angel Vision as showing 'unusual moments in baseball' — sounds like a standard stadium entertainment segment
jokes.punchline: The footage shown (inferred from the extended gap 64:40–65:05 and the apologetic 'Sorry, fellas!') is clearly something inappropriate or absurd — likely bloopers or an embarrassing clip — culminating in the announcer sheepishly apologizing
jokes.explanation: A ZAZ visual gag that depends entirely on the film image rather than dialogue. The transcript gives us the setup and the apologetic aftermath, strongly implying the Angel Vision played something embarrassing or off-color. Rewatch value is high because the visual payoff is in the film itself.

jokes.text: 'Sorry, fellas!' — Frank on the field, clearly having disrupted something during the Angel Vision segment or warm-ups, apologizing with complete nonchalance.
jokes.setup: Some chaotic physical mishap has just occurred involving Frank on or near the field.
jokes.punchline: His breezy, one-line apology massively undersells whatever disaster he caused.
jokes.explanation: Pure Leslie Nielsen/Frank Drebin economy — maximum disaster, minimum acknowledgment. The deadpan understatement is the entire joke and it works because of Nielsen's established persona.

jokes.text: PA announcement: 'For everybody's safety, we ask that you do not throw any objects on the field. We thank you for your co-operation.' — immediately after the Queen is introduced to applause
jokes.setup: Standard, polite stadium PA safety announcement delivered in a cheerful, rote tone
jokes.punchline: The timing — right after introducing the Queen of England as the first-pitch thrower — implies the announcement is a veiled warning that someone might actually try to assassinate her with a thrown object, but it's delivered as though it's the usual 'don't throw beach balls' notice
jokes.explanation: ZAZ at its most economical — a completely normal announcement that lands as darkly funny given the assassination plot context. The joke is entirely structural: position in the film does the heavy lifting. Economy score is high because there's no extra word.

jokes.text: 'These lovely ladies would agree — those are the players' wives, here to enjoy the game.' The wives are visually comedic (implied: they look nothing like the announcer's flattering description)
jokes.setup: Announcer refers to 'these lovely ladies' in a gallant, game-show-host tone
jokes.punchline: The camera reveals the players' wives look decidedly un-lovely — ZAZ's signature bait-and-switch between complimentary narration and unflattering image
jokes.explanation: A reliable ZAZ formula — the voiceover says one thing, the image contradicts it. It's a bit cheap (relies on the audience laughing at people's appearances) but structurally clean and efficiently executed.

jokes.text: "What d'you say, Cummings? Are we gonna do this today?" / "Do what?" / "Play ball!"
jokes.setup: Frank (as umpire) addresses the catcher with what sounds like tough-guy cop talk: 'Are we gonna do this today?'
jokes.punchline: The catcher's confused 'Do what?' forces Frank to clarify — 'Play ball!' — revealing the intimidating phrasing was just literal umpire talk, deflating any tension while making Frank seem oblivious to how he sounds
jokes.explanation: A compact three-line exchange that works perfectly. Frank's hard-boiled cop phrasing accidentally sounds like a threatening negotiation, the straight-man catcher's literal question punctures it, and the mundane payoff ('Play ball!') is exactly the right anticlimax. Good economy — no wasted words.

jokes.text: Frank stops Jay Johnstone mid-at-bat to check if his uniform is 'on straight' and inspect his shirt, telling him 'You should take a large. It's a little tight in the crotch.'
jokes.setup: Frank (as umpire) is supposed to be officiating; instead he's conducting a bizarre personal inspection of the batter's uniform sizing while play waits
jokes.punchline: 'You should take a large. It's a little tight in the crotch.' — Frank delivers a tailor's intimate observation with total deadpan authority, treating a sizing complaint as official umpire business
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's standout gags. Only Frank Drebin — blissfully unaware of social norms — would stop a World Series-level game to comment on a player's crotch fit with the seriousness of an official ruling. Nielsen's deadpan delivery is baked into the writing. The specificity ('You should take a large') elevates it beyond generic inappropriateness into something truly original. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor — sharp, unexpected, perfectly economical.

jokes.text: 'All right? All set?' — Frank finishes frisking/inspecting the batter and cheerfully clears him to hit, as if completing a routine safety check
jokes.setup: After the bizarre uniform inspection, Frank seems to have concluded his 'official' duties
jokes.punchline: The cheerful, bureaucratic sign-off ('All right? All set?') treats the whole absurd interaction as standard procedure, heightening the obliviousness
jokes.explanation: A button on joke #6 — the cheerful procedural sign-off extends the absurdity but doesn't add new comedic information. Gets credit for the escalation but mostly coasts on the momentum of the previous beat.

jokes.text: Frank calls a strike — then reacts with surprise himself: 'Strike?' / 'Yeah, strike!' — the umpire is startled by his own call
jokes.setup: Frank makes the strike call in his umpire role
jokes.punchline: He immediately questions his own call ('Strike?') as if he didn't expect it, then confirms it only when echoed back — suggesting he's making it up as he goes
jokes.explanation: A deceptively simple gag that lands hard. An umpire questioning his own call is inherently absurd, but the rhythm — Frank says 'Strike?', the catcher confirms it, Frank doubles down — reveals Frank is operating purely on the fly with no actual knowledge of the sport. Perfect character integration: only Drebin could bungle competence this specifically.

jokes.text: Extended visual sequence: Frank calls three strikes while simultaneously conducting a full pat-down frisk of the batter through each pitch
jokes.setup: Frank needs to frisk every player while also umpiring; the game keeps going and he has to do both simultaneously
jokes.punchline: Visual comedy of Frank running through frisk procedures (checking pockets, feeling for weapons, inspecting shoes) between each pitch, treating the game as an inconvenient interruption to his police work
jokes.explanation: The sustained physical comedy of Frank frisking players between pitches — with real major-league players complying — is a pure ZAZ set piece. The gap from 69:01 to 69:56 implies an extended visual sequence. The joke is in the sustained commitment: Frank doesn't rush; the game accommodates his police work. High rewatch value because physical comedy rewards multiple viewings.

jokes.text: 'You're clean!' — Frank's verdict after a full examination of the batter, delivered as a police clearance rather than a baseball call
jokes.setup: Frank has completed his inspection of a batter; the batter and crowd await his ruling
jokes.punchline: 'You're clean!' — the definitive cop clearance delivered in the umpire context, with Drebin apparently satisfied the player isn't the assassin
jokes.explanation: Two words that do an enormous amount of work. 'You're clean' is simultaneously the cop's standard drug-search verdict and an absurdly wrong umpire call — it means nothing in baseball but Frank delivers it with absolute authority. It's the perfect payoff to the entire frisking sequence. Maximum economy (two words), perfect character integration, and genuinely quotable. Earns its 8.5 — it's the kind of line that becomes the representative quote for the whole sequence.

jokes.text: Al reveals Frank has 'searched almost everybody' but there's 'only one more out before the seventh inning stretch' — meaning Frank has been frisking players for most of the game
jokes.setup: Frank has been conducting his undercover search throughout the game; Al checks in on progress
jokes.punchline: The sheer volume implied — 'almost everybody' across both teams over multiple innings — retroactively makes the earlier frisking gags even bigger. Frank has apparently searched dozens of professional athletes at a Major League game and nobody stopped him
jokes.explanation: This line functions as a callback that expands the scale of all the earlier frisking gags retroactively. The comedy is in the implication: Frank has somehow searched most of a professional baseball roster during a live game. Good escalation structure — the reveal of scope is the punchline.

jokes.text: Al tells Frank he needs to 'stall them — don't let 'em get that third out' so he can finish his search
jokes.setup: Frank needs more time; the inning is almost over
jokes.punchline: The instruction 'don't let them get the third out' means Frank — a fake umpire with no baseball knowledge — has to actively sabotage the game's natural progression to stall. The absurdity of a cop being tasked with manipulating a Major League Baseball game is the joke
jokes.explanation: An excellent premise setup for the extended chaos to follow. The joke is in the logical absurdity of the solution — the best way to protect the Queen is to corrupt an MLB game. It's a strong bridge joke that earns its score by powering the best visual sequence in the reel.

jokes.text: Frank calls 'Ball!' on a pitch — then again at 72:31 — then again, stalling for time by calling everything a ball regardless of where it was thrown
jokes.setup: Frank has been told to prevent the third out; his method is to call every pitch a ball to extend the at-bat indefinitely
jokes.punchline: The repeated 'Ball!' calls, escalating in confidence, suggest Frank has found his preferred method of stalling — essentially veto-ing the entire concept of strikes. The pitcher and catcher presumably react with increasing outrage
jokes.explanation: The visual/audio gag of Frank calling every pitch a ball with growing authority is a good escalation beat. Each repeated 'Ball!' represents Frank doubling down on his incompetent stall tactic with Drebin-esque certainty.

jokes.text: 'Get... get... what the? Get off!' — chaos erupts on the field; Frank appears to have caused a physical scuffle while trying to stall
jokes.setup: Frank's increasingly aggressive stalling has escalated beyond ball calls to some form of physical intervention on the field
jokes.punchline: Frank's confused, escalating commands ('Get... get... what the?') suggest he's wrestling with someone or something that wasn't part of his plan — the stall has spiraled into full physical chaos
jokes.explanation: Primarily a visual gag — the specific dialogue is fragmented because the comedy is in what the audience sees. The escalating physical chaos is classic ZAZ but this beat reads better on screen than on the page.

jokes.text: The umpires themselves get into the rundown — 'It's hard to believe, but apparently the umpires have got Criscione in a run-down!'
jokes.setup: A rundown (a player caught between bases) is a standard baseball play executed by fielders
jokes.punchline: The umpires — specifically Frank — are apparently executing the rundown themselves, which is entirely against the rules and physically insane. The announcer's deadpan 'apparently' acknowledges he doesn't believe it either
jokes.explanation: The announcer's 'apparently' is doing tremendous work — it's the voice of a reasonable person watching something physically impossible unfold. The image of umpires chasing a baserunner between bases is so wrong it becomes transcendently funny. The escalation from 'calling balls' to 'physically participating in the game' is perfectly ZAZ. Strong originality: I can't name another film gag quite like it.

jokes.text: Multiple umpires arguing 'Safe! / Out!' with each other — then Frank ejects another umpire — 'You can't throw an umpire out!' / 'All right, YOU'RE out!' — then argues with the scoreboard operator
jokes.setup: Umpires disagreeing is normal; Frank has taken his stalling to the point of actively contradicting fellow officials
jokes.punchline: Frank ejects an umpire from the game — something that has never happened in baseball — then when told he can't do that, ejects the person who told him. Then disputes the scoreboard. Each escalation is more impossible than the last
jokes.explanation: This is the reel's comedic peak. The escalation structure is immaculate: safe/out disagreement → umpire ejected by another umpire → that person ejected for protesting → scoreboard dispute. Each step is more absurd than the last and each is a logical extension of Frank's oblivious authority. The 'You can't throw an umpire out!' / 'All right, YOU'RE out!' exchange is particularly sharp — it's almost a perfect mini setup/punchline with Frank applying his only known tool (ejection) to solve every obstacle. Approaches the 9+ anchor territory for craft.

jokes.text: 'How could you do something so vicious?' / 'It was easy. Don't forget I spent two years as a building contractor.'
jokes.setup: Frank confronts the villain/killer with the accusation 'How could you do something so vicious?' — implying he means the assassination plot
jokes.punchline: The killer's response ('It was easy — I spent two years as a building contractor') pivots to an entirely unrelated, deadpan dark joke implying building contractors are routinely vicious — a non-sequitur that also works as a real-world joke about contractor culture
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in ZAZ misdirection and economy. The question sets up an answer about murder/evil; instead the villain deflects to a mundane professional background that somehow makes perfect sense as a dark joke. 'Don't forget I spent two years as a building contractor' has an almost Pythonesque quality — the specificity (two years, not one, not 'a while') makes it land harder. Highly quotable, genuinely original. Comfortably in 8+ territory.

jokes.text: 'Hey, look at that! Let's get him!' — the crowd spots Frank chasing/escorting the villain and spontaneously joins in
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to quietly remove the villain from the stadium ('let's go quietly')
jokes.punchline: The crowd spots whatever Frank is doing and mob mentality kicks in — they join the chase, completely derailing his plan for a quiet arrest
jokes.explanation: A reliable but not exceptional crowd-chaos gag. Works as a ZAZ escalation but doesn't add new comedic logic — it's just 'thing spirals into bigger thing,' which is a bit generic compared to the more inventive gags in this reel.

jokes.text: 'Kick him in the balls!' — a spectator's specific, enthusiastic instruction during the chaotic crowd chase
jokes.setup: The crowd has joined the chase; a spectator shouts an instruction
jokes.punchline: The instruction is surprisingly specific, violent, and enthusiastic — the kind of suggestion only an extremely invested (possibly drunk) baseball fan would shout, and it comes out of nowhere in the chaos
jokes.explanation: A quick, cheap laugh that works on pure unexpectedness — it's the right level of wrong for a ZAZ film but it's not particularly crafted. Functions as an escalation beat more than a standalone joke.

jokes.text: 'The umpire... He saved the Queen's life!' / 'That's not the umpire, Your Honour.'
jokes.setup: Frank (in umpire costume) has just saved the Queen; the announcer thinks he's an actual umpire
jokes.punchline: Al corrects the record — but the correction implies the audience still doesn't fully know who Frank is, and 'Your Honour' is a funny mix of titles suggesting confusion about Frank's exact role
jokes.explanation: A clean callback payoff to the undercover umpire premise. The 'Your Honour' address is a small bonus joke embedded in the correction. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: 'Hey, it's Enrico Pallazzo!' — the crowd recognizes Frank in his opera singer disguise (from an earlier reel)
jokes.setup: Frank has been undercover as the famous opera singer Enrico Pallazzo at the stadium
jokes.punchline: The crowd collectively recognizes 'Enrico Pallazzo' — meaning Frank's disguise was apparently convincing enough that everyone in the stadium believes he's a famous tenor, which is a callback to his earlier impersonation
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback that works on multiple levels: Frank's idiotic disguise somehow fooled an entire stadium, and the crowd's warm recognition is the perfect absurd payoff. The name 'Enrico Pallazzo' has become one of the film's most quoted lines, indicating its cultural resonance exceeds what the transcript alone suggests.

jokes.text: 'He's got a gun.' / 'I know.'
jokes.setup: Al warns Frank urgently that Ludwig (the villain) has a gun
jokes.punchline: Frank's flat 'I know' — delivered without alarm, as though Al has told him something mildly interesting — is perfect Drebin deadpan. He is staring down a gun barrel and is essentially unimpressed
jokes.explanation: Two words that capture everything about Frank Drebin. 'He's got a gun' / 'I know' is the purest expression of Drebin deadpan — maximum economy, perfect character integration, and the gap between the urgency of the situation and his total lack of reaction is the entire joke. Nielsen's delivery must be magnificent here. Economy scores a 10: literally cannot be shorter.

jokes.text: 'Leave the girl alone!' / 'I am. I'm going to kill you.'
jokes.setup: Frank heroically demands the villain leave Jane alone
jokes.punchline: The villain points out he is, in fact, leaving the girl alone — his plan is to kill Frank, not Jane. The villain is technically correct, which is the best kind of correct, and deflates Frank's heroic moment completely
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed two-line exchange. Frank's heroic line sets up an expected confrontation; the villain's literal, technically-correct reply ('I am — I'm going to kill you') is both funny and genuinely menacing. It deflates Frank's hero posture while making the villain seem oddly reasonable. High originality — the punchline is in the villain's pedantic clarification, which is a subversion of the expected villain monologue format.

jokes.text: 'Two can play at that game!' — Frank brandishes what is presumably a comically inadequate weapon in response to being threatened with a gun
jokes.setup: Frank faces a gunman; needs to respond with equal or greater force
jokes.punchline: 'Two can play at that game!' announces a symmetrical threat — but Frank's weapon is presumably absurdly outmatched (a visual gag). The confident cliché delivered against clearly unequal odds is the Drebin signature
jokes.explanation: The joke lives in the visual payoff (what exactly Frank produces), which the transcript can't capture. The line itself is a funny cliché deployed with Drebin confidence, but the full impact requires the film image.

jokes.text: 'You killed him!' / 'No, just stunned. He'll be all right.'
jokes.setup: Jane sees the villain apparently drop after Frank acts; she assumes he's dead
jokes.punchline: Frank's calm 'No, just stunned. He'll be all right.' is an absurd medical diagnosis delivered with total authority — as though Frank can determine from a glance that someone is merely 'stunned' after being shot/hit
jokes.explanation: Classic Drebin reassurance — delivered with the same certainty whether he's right or wrong. 'Just stunned' is a funny understatement for what appears to be a potentially lethal confrontation. The 'he'll be all right' adds a breezy unconcern that's very on-brand.

jokes.text: 'It's so horrible!' / 'I know, Ed.' / 'My father went the same way.'
jokes.setup: Ed is visibly distressed; Frank commiserates with 'I know, Ed' — the audience assumes they're discussing the near-assassination or the chaos
jokes.punchline: 'My father went the same way' — Frank reveals he's talking about something entirely personal and unrelated, implying his father also died in some bizarre baseball-stadium/assassination-adjacent fashion, or more likely pivoting to a completely irrelevant personal trauma
jokes.explanation: A compact misdirection gag — Frank's empathetic response ('I know, Ed') sounds appropriate, then 'My father went the same way' recontextualizes it as Frank making the moment about himself with a completely irrelevant personal tragedy. It's a small but well-crafted beat. The specificity ('went the same way') implies some absurd off-screen backstory.

jokes.text: Jane, apparently hypnotized/brainwashed, keeps intoning 'I must kill... Frank Drebin' — a villain's trigger phrase she keeps repeating throughout the confrontation
jokes.setup: Jane has been programmed as an assassin; her brainwashing manifests as a repeated monotone declaration
jokes.punchline: The repeated 'I must kill... Frank Drebin' — with its dramatic ellipsis — becomes increasingly funny as Frank tries to woo her back while she keeps announcing her intention to murder him
jokes.explanation: The running gag of Jane robotically announcing murder intentions while Frank delivers romantic speeches is a good sustained joke. The comedy increases with each repetition because Frank's obliviousness to the threat grows more absurd — he's giving a Casablanca speech to someone pointing a gun at him.

jokes.text: 'Funny-face.'
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to reach Jane through her brainwashing; he needs to snap her out of a murder trance
jokes.punchline: His chosen term of endearment — 'Funny-face' — is both sweet and slightly odd, delivered with the same gravity as if he were defusing a bomb. The timing (she's just said 'I must kill Frank Drebin') makes the gentle nickname absurdly inappropriate yet somehow perfect
jokes.explanation: One word that does enormous work. 'Funny-face' is exactly the kind of earnest, slightly-off term of endearment that only Drebin would use in a life-threatening situation. It's not ironic — he means it — which makes it funnier. High character integration because it's so specifically Drebin's register of romance.

jokes.text: Frank delivers a romantic speech to Jane about how much he loves her — while she repeatedly announces 'I must kill Frank Drebin' between his lines
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to break Jane's hypnotic programming with declarations of love; she keeps announcing her intention to kill him
jokes.punchline: The juxtaposition of Frank's heartfelt romantic speech and Jane's monotone murder announcements creates escalating cringe comedy — especially 'Jane, if you don't love me, you might as well pull that trigger, because without you, I wouldn't want to live anyway'
jokes.explanation: The 'you might as well pull that trigger' line is the standout — it accidentally aligns Frank's romantic despair with Jane's literal murder plan, making his declaration of devotion sound like permission. It's sustained cringe comedy with a brilliant structural peak in that line.

jokes.text: Frank's speech to dissuade Jane: 'You love Frank Drebin. And Frank Drebin loves you.' — referring to himself in the third person while Jane holds a gun to him
jokes.setup: Frank tries to break Jane's hypnosis by reminding her of their love.
jokes.punchline: He refers to himself in the third person — 'Frank Drebin loves you' — as if he is an objective fact that must be stated for the record, not a person speaking about his own feelings.
jokes.explanation: The third-person self-reference is a subtle character comedy beat — Frank is so formal and procedural that even his love declaration becomes a police report. Works well in context of the scene.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Jane, if you don't love me, you might as well pull that trigger, because without you, I wouldn't want to live anyway.'
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to persuade Jane not to shoot him, but his romantic declaration accidentally endorses the shooting.
jokes.punchline: The logic of 'if you don't love me, pull the trigger' is a romantic cliché that also happens to be a sincere death wish, delivered to someone actively trying to kill him. He's literally giving the assassin permission.
jokes.explanation: Smart dark comedy — the romantic movie line ('I wouldn't want to live anyway') is literally being said to someone pointing a gun at him. The double meaning is intentional and well-constructed. Frank is both making a sincere declaration and accidentally providing justification for his own murder.

jokes.text: 'I've finally found someone I can love — a good, clean love... without utensils.'
jokes.setup: Frank is delivering a romantic declaration of love
jokes.punchline: '...without utensils.' — a completely inexplicable qualifier that derails the entire speech. What utensils? Why are utensils relevant to love? The specificity of the non-sequitur is the entire joke
jokes.explanation: One of the great ZAZ non-sequiturs and arguably the best joke in this reel. The setup is a sincere romantic speech — 'a good, clean love' has a wholesome, almost naive ring — then 'without utensils' arrives like a bomb. The phrase is specific enough to imply a whole backstory (previous loves that DID involve utensils?) but vague enough to be completely inexplicable. It's infinitely quotable, structurally immaculate, and could only come from a writer who understood that the best absurdist non-sequiturs sound almost plausible. Comparable to the 9+ anchor in cultural resonance and craft.

jokes.text: 'It's a topsy-turvy world, Jane, and maybe the problems of two people don't amount to a hill of beans, but this is our hill and these are our beans.'
jokes.setup: Frank is paraphrasing the famous Casablanca 'hill of beans' speech — 'the problems of three little people don't amount to a hill of beans in this crazy world'
jokes.punchline: Frank literalizes the metaphor — 'but this IS our hill and these ARE our beans' — missing the entire point of Casablanca's self-sacrifice theme and instead making it about territorial possession of a bean hill. The misunderstanding reveals Drebin's earnest literalism
jokes.explanation: A masterful parody that works on two levels: it's funny as a standalone absurd image (Frank and Jane's bean hill), and it's funnier if you know Casablanca because Frank has completely inverted the meaning — Bogart was saying they don't matter; Frank is saying they DO matter and furthermore the beans are his. The literalization of a cliché is a ZAZ specialty and this is one of their best executions. Earns its near-9 — it's distinctive, perfectly structured, and highly quotable.

jokes.text: 'Since I met you, I've noticed things I never knew were there — birds singing, dew glistening on a newly-formed leaf, stop lights...'
jokes.setup: Frank lists beautiful things love has made him notice — a classic romantic trope
jokes.punchline: '...stop lights.' The poetic list (birds, dew, newly-formed leaf) crashes into the mundane and urgent ('stop lights') — implying Frank has been running red lights his whole career and love has finally made him comply with traffic law
jokes.explanation: One of the best written lines in this reel. The list setup is perfect — 'birds singing, dew glistening on a newly-formed leaf' is genuinely lyrical, which makes the crash-landing of 'stop lights' even more devastating. The ellipsis before it in the transcript captures the comedic pause. The joke is also character-specific: Frank is a cop who has presumably been breaking traffic laws his whole career and love has finally made him notice basic road safety. Structural perfection and excellent economy — 'stop lights' is the ideal word to end that list.

jokes.text: 'I must kill...' [Jane's voice] — interrupting Frank's speech again, then fading before she completes it — suggesting the programming is breaking
jokes.setup: Jane has been repeatedly saying 'I must kill Frank Drebin' throughout the scene
jokes.punchline: This time she starts but doesn't finish — the speech is working. The incomplete murder announcement is both funny and weirdly touching
jokes.explanation: A structural beat in the running gag rather than a standalone joke — the incomplete declaration signals the arc of the scene. Gets credit for the structural function but doesn't add new comedic material.

jokes.text: Frank produces an engagement ring and explains: 'I'd have given it to you earlier, but I wanted to wait until we were alone.' — they are in a stadium with the Queen, security, and thousands of fans
jokes.setup: Frank presents an engagement ring to Jane with the explanation that he waited for a private moment
jokes.punchline: They are surrounded by an enormous crowd, the Queen of England, security forces, and a stadium full of people — 'until we were alone' is maximally ironic. Frank genuinely seems to think this counts as alone
jokes.explanation: Frank's obliviousness to his surroundings is so complete that proposing marriage in a packed stadium 'because we're finally alone' perfectly encapsulates his character. The joke rewards knowing the setting — a callback to the entire stadium environment. Strong character integration: only Drebin would see a crowd of 50,000 as an intimate setting.

jokes.text: Frank produces an engagement ring: 'It's not very much, but pretty good for an honest policeman's salary.'
jokes.setup: Frank reveals he has an engagement ring — a grand romantic gesture.
jokes.punchline: He immediately pre-emptively apologizes for its quality, citing 'an honest policeman's salary' — the qualifier 'honest' doing quiet work implying he considered a less honest approach.
jokes.explanation: The word 'honest' is quietly doing a lot here — Frank specifying his salary is from an 'honest' policeman implies he considered corruption and chose not to, which is both a character reveal and a commentary on police corruption played entirely straight. The self-deprecating ring apology is sweet and funny simultaneously. High character integration: this is exactly what Frank Drebin would say while proposing.

jokes.text: Mayor: 'I was wrong about you. This city and the whole world owes you a debt of gratitude.' — Frank had been fired/dismissed earlier in the film; this is his vindication
jokes.setup: The Mayor had presumably doubted or fired Frank; now comes to apologize
jokes.punchline: The grandiosity of 'the whole world owes you a debt of gratitude' for a man who stumbled through the entire plot causing chaos is the joke — Frank's vindication is completely unearned from an objective standpoint. The Mayor's straight-faced delivery of maximum praise for a man who accidentally saved the day
jokes.explanation: A satisfying structural beat but not a strong individual joke. The irony is that Frank deserves none of the praise being heaped on him, but this is implicit rather than explicitly funny. Works better as plot resolution than comedy.

jokes.text: Nordberg appears — apparently fully recovered from being shot repeatedly at the start of the film — 'The doc says I should be on my feet in a week! And back on the Force!'
jokes.setup: Nordberg was shot multiple times in the opening sequence of the film and was hospitalized
jokes.punchline: Nordberg is here, mobile, cheerful, and apparently recovering well from what were portrayed as life-threatening injuries — the impossible resilience is the joke. The optimistic 'back on the Force!' from someone who should probably be dead is classic dark ZAZ
jokes.explanation: A satisfying full-film callback that lands because the audience has waited the entire movie for Nordberg's fate. The cheerful 'back on the Force!' from someone who had seemingly unsurvivable injuries is a good dark comedy beat. O.J. Simpson's casting adds a layer of irony the film couldn't have intended.

jokes.text: 'Frank! Everyone should have a friend like you!'
jokes.setup: Nordberg warmly praises Frank's friendship
jokes.punchline: Frank's 'friendship' led directly to Nordberg being shot nearly to death, hospitalized for the entire film, and subjected to numerous additional physical disasters in earlier reels. The praise is maximally undeserved, which is the joke
jokes.explanation: A good closing joke — the warmth of Nordberg's praise is inversely proportional to how terrible Frank has been for his health. It's a satisfying dark button on the Nordberg running gag. The line is quotable precisely because the irony is so complete.
